27: ## Identity
28: The project is **Gilbert** — a distinct application, backronym for
29: **G**eneral-purpose **I**ntelligent **L**ifecycle **B**utler for
30: **E**nterprise **R**esource **T**raceability. Its mail client is based on
31: upstream ihasmail (Coffey Labs), which is download-only (ADR 0002): releases
32: sync in, nothing goes back. Canonical statement: README.md top.
33: 
34: ## Snapshot mode
35: Files and comments describe the code as it is now. Never write "it used to
36: be X, then it became Y", never narrate a rename, a migration or any
37: before/after. **A document is edited in place**: when what it describes
38: changes, the sentence changes with it in the same diff, and the version it
39: replaced is left to git rather than kept beside it or pointed at. If somebody
40: wants history, it is in git.
41: 
42: ## Naming rule
43: The product has four blocks, named once in `README.md`: **gilbertmailer**,
44: **gilbertserver**, **gilbertagents** and **gilbertstalwart**. Every doc, ADR
45: and skill names them that way and does not redefine them; a new document links
46: to the README rather than restating it. Only `gilbertmailer`, and inside
47: `gilbertserver` the layer that serves it, come from upstream — the rest is
48: Gilbert's own, and the README states that line once.
49: Prose about the product says "Gilbert", and every code and build identifier
50: is `gilbert`: `APP_NAME` default "Gilbert", packages `gilbert`/`@gilbert/*`,
51: `GILBERT_VERSION`, `X-Requested-With: gilbert`, UI strings and catalogs, the
52: app folder, the sieve script name, storage keys, the `[gilbert]` log prefix,
53: the `session.gilbert` extension, MIME types, docker/deploy identifiers and
54: paths. `ihasmail` appears only where upstream's real name must stay: the AGPL
55: attribution in `LICENSE`/`NOTICE` — `NOTICE` being the only file that carries
56: its addresses (ihasmail.org, docs.ihasmail.org, git.coffeylabs.org/coffey-labs/ihasmail,
57: and its GitHub-era ihasmail-github-archive) — and the lineage prose in
58: `README`/ADR 0002, which names upstream and points at `NOTICE`. No public doc
59: carries a link to upstream: `README`, `FEATURES.md`, `KNOWN-ISSUES.md`,
60: `ROADMAP.md` and the ADRs name it plainly, cite an issue number as a plain
61: number, and send the reader to `NOTICE` for the address.
62: An upstream merge delta that introduces `ihasmail` identifiers, strings or
63: prose is renamed to `gilbert`/`Gilbert` during the merge, automatically and
64: without asking — including user-visible names such as a shipped theme or
65: palette id. Only the upstream-name exceptions above may stay.
66: 
67: The agent vocabulary is three words and they are not synonyms. One **Master**
68: is the principal everything belongs to: the account in Stalwart
69: (`gilbert@…`), its address, its password, its grants, and the model it uses. Its
70: **agent** is the process that acts as it, and it runs inside `gilbertserver`.
71: **Worker** is kept for what is technically one: the browser's service worker —
72: an unqualified "worker" is that, and never the agent.
73: 
74: **The identifiers follow the same three words** — the file, the types and the
75: functions on one side, and
76: on the other the things that are contracts rather than names: a field in a
77: document an installation has already written, a refusal code a client composes a
78: sentence from, an environment variable an operator set. Each moves with every
79: reader and writer of it in the same change, or it does not move at all.
80: ## Architecture law
81: JMAP only, to Stalwart; no own database; everything durable lives in Stalwart;
82: container disposable; `IMMUTABLE=1` = no writable filesystem. Values: fail
83: loudly, degrade gracefully by capability, sanitise HTML, settings follow the
84: account (localStorage is only a cache).
85: 
86: ## Architecture decisions (ADR)
87: Decisions that shape the architecture — where durable state lives, a protocol
88: surface, a trust boundary, an enforcement door, or a documented invariant —
89: are recorded as Architecture Decision Records under `docs/adr/`, one file per
90: decision: `NNNN-kebab-case-title.md` starting at `0001`, written in English,
91: with a `Status` line (Proposed / Accepted) and an `Implementation` line, then
92: Context, Decision and Consequences sections.
93: **`Status` is where the decision stands; `Implementation` is where the tree
94: stands.** Both are required, and each opens a short paragraph rather than a
95: single line:
96: `Status` moves only when the owner accepts a decision — it is a judgement, not a
97: build state — and it never carries a date or a note about what an earlier
98: version said. `Implementation` says whether the tree carries the decision and
99: names what does: `Built.` with the paths, `Built and live-verified.` for a
100: behaviour confirmed against a live Stalwart, `Built, and carried by …` when the
101: repository's own shape rather than code carries it, `Partly built.` naming what
102: is carried and what is not, or `Not built.` A record whose implementation is
103: owed the live probe it depends on says so in its body, and `ROADMAP.md` carries
104: what is planned. Neither is a changelog: the version before this commit is git's.
105: Write the ADR when the change is designed, before or alongside the
106: implementation, so the design is reviewable first; an implementation must
107: match the ADR that covers it. ADRs stay `Proposed` until the owner accepts them.
108: **A record is edited in place, and the history is git's.** Changing a standing
109: decision means rewriting the record that carries it, in the change that alters
110: it, until it states the decision as it now stands: never a second record that
111: supersedes the first, never a `Superseded` status, never a sentence narrating
112: what the earlier version said or what used to be true. A number is minted for a
113: decision that is new, not for a version of one already here. The single
114: exception is the owner asking for otherwise, explicitly and in the turn: only
115: then does a decision get a record beside the existing one instead of a rewrite
116: of it.
117: **Snapshot mode applies to the ADRs too, and a resolution carries no
118: back-reference.** It states the decision and the facts it rests on — never the
119: conversation that produced it: no "the first/second/third branch review found",
120: no "the review raised", no "as the reviews recommended". Resolution numbers,
121: dates, `Owed:` markers and every fact stay exactly as they are; what goes is the
122: reference to the round that argued it. A reader of the record is reading
123: decisions, not a diary — the history is in git.

125: ## Toolchain
126: Node ≥ 24, npm workspaces. **Node runs on the latest LTS line, and the line is
127: the one the deployment pins** (`Dockerfile` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` say
128: 24). A Current release is never supported, and `@types/node` follows the pinned
129: line rather than the newest published one: typing against a release nobody
130: deploys describes a Node this project does not run. Moving the line is a
131: deliberate change of all of it at once (image, CI, engines, types), never a
132: Dependabot bump.
133: 
134: ```bash
135: npm run dev:mock        # full stack, mock Stalwart, demo@example.com / demo
136: npm run dev             # a real Stalwart (STALWART_URL in .env)
137: npm run typecheck       # tsc, both packages
138: npm test                # vitest (web) + node:test (server)
139: npm run build           # web/dist, then server/dist
140: ```
141: 
142: One test, not the suite: `npm run test -w web -- src/lib/<name>.test.ts`
143: (vitest), or from `server/` `npx tsx --test src/<name>.test.ts` (node:test).
144: **Lint + format gate: Biome** (`biome.jsonc` — calibrated to this repo's
145: actual style, with deliberate, commented rule exceptions; a11y off). Run with
146: `npm run lint` / `npm run lint:fix`; it is part of `check:ci`, run by the
147: pre-push hook and by the CI release pre-check.
148: **The gate reports zero, or it has not passed (global user rule, active here).**
149: "Pre-existing" is not a category: every error, warning and informational finding
150: the gate prints is fixed, whoever wrote the line and whenever it arrived — and a
151: non-zero count is work to do, never context to report. Biome 0/0/0, no failing
152: test, no skipped test, a dependency audit at zero (the release pre-check runs
153: `npm run audit`).
154: **Tests assume the runner's local timezone is UTC** (GitHub's default); on a
155: non-UTC machine run them as `TZ=UTC npm test` — `check:ci` already forces it so
156: the local gate matches CI.
157: **`npm run check:ci` is the one gate**, in order: typecheck, Biome, `adr:owed`,
158: `adr:cite`, `config:dead`, `workflow:pin`, `i18n:check`, `TZ=UTC npm test`, then
159: `npm run build`. The pre-push hook runs it (`npm run prepush` is that pipeline
160: under the name the hook calls), and
161: `ci.yml` runs the same script — so the release pre-check and a developer's push
162: cannot diverge. The only part of CI that is not in it is the Docker smoke build,
163: which a local gate cannot assume has a daemon.
164: Version from git at build time (`node scripts/version.mjs`).

166: ## Language
167: Code comments, documentation, commit messages and every other file in the repo
168: are written in **English**. Never write or translate repo content into another
169: language. Chat replies follow the user's language — the chat is not repo
170: content.

172: ## Workflow
173: Read the affected area first; smallest coherent diff.
174: **A dev stack you start, you stop (owner decision 2026-09-24).** Anything
175: launched to exercise the tree — the mock Stalwart, the dev server, Vite, a
176: container — is killed when the work that needed it is done, in that turn. A
177: process left listening holds ports the next run needs and looks like a working
178: deployment to whoever finds it next; leave one running only when the owner says
179: so in that same turn. This outranks the convenience of a warm stack: it is one
180: command to start again.
181: **Load the skill that governs the work before the first edit of it (global user
182: rule, active here — owner decision 2026-09-18).** The list at the end of this
183: file says which skill a kind of work belongs to, and `gilbert-project` is loaded
184: at the start of any task here. A skill read afterwards is a skill that did not do
185: its job: it is where a convention this file states once is written out in full,
186: and the cost of skipping it is a change rewritten against rules that were already
187: written down.
188: **A unit of work is committed when it is finished — automatically (owner decision
189: 2026-09-24):** each unit lands as it is finished — not at the end of the turn,
190: and not once a review has been answered — and **without the user asking for the
191: commit in the turn**: this repository commits per unit on its own, superseding
192: the global "no commit unless asked" rule for this tree. A unit is one coherent
193: change — a rule with its guard and its test, a document with the sentences the
194: change falsified, an i18n fix with the catalogs it emptied — and it lands with
195: its own message. Work held back until a review or a turn's end becomes a
196: mega-commit whose message cannot say what it did and whose parts cannot be read
197: apart. What is **not** part of the unit is its check: only biome/tsc run, at the
198: end of the turn (the rule below), so a unit commit is the change and its message
199: and nothing else.
200: **Single source of truth, no code duplication (global user rule, owner-confirmed
201: 2026-09-08):** within the same artifact type — code↔code and docs↔docs — every
202: concept, constant, classifier, schema and helper has one canonical definition;
203: everything else imports or derives from it. The rule does not cross the
204: docs↔code boundary: docs may duplicate values from the code or a config to stay
205: self-contained and readable. Before writing a new definition, search for the
206: existing one; a found duplicate is deleted and routed through the canonical
207: source in the same change.
208: **Dispatched sub-agents are health-checked automatically, never on request:**
209: poll each running agent at least every ~60 s (steps advancing, live tool
210: calls, processes, worktree writes / file mtimes). An agent with no progress
211: across consecutive polls, or that dies or is cancelled, is investigated and
212: replaced or recovered immediately — never left until the user notices.
213: **Cost and time discipline (global user rule, active here):** agents read only
214: the diff hunks under review plus the functions they directly call — targeted
215: grep/sed/read slices, never whole large files; review agents do not run full
216: test suites (the parent runs the gate); large reviews are split into small
217: parallel reviewers by area; deep reasoning is reserved for security-critical
218: surfaces. An agent that drifts into wide exploration gets a converge-now
219: instruction rather than being left to widen scope.
220: **Diagnosis: measure once, on what runs (global user rule, active here).** A
221: measurement is trusted only after the thing it meant to provoke is proved to
222: have happened (the route changed, the action fired, the state moved); behaviour
223: questions are measured against the code that runs — the built bundle the
224: deployment serves, the real latency, the real data — not the dev server when the
225: report came from production. One attempt per tool: a capture that does not
226: produce the datum on the first try (screencast, profiler without screenshots, a
227: trace without the track needed) is dropped for the cheapest source that answers
228: the question, usually a count over the DOM. Diagnosis → the smallest fix →
229: verification, with no exploration in between; what was tried and abandoned is
230: said in the report, never pursued.
231: **Reviewer dispatch (owner decision 2026-09-09):** every review is split into small parallel reviewers by
232: area, each with an explicit bounded file list, a diff range limited to the
233: change under review (never a stale merge-base that drags unrelated history
234: in), a tool-call budget stated in the prompt (~12), and the read-only grammar
235: preamble. Poll reviewer agents and act on the first anomalous poll — one past
236: budget or burning tokens on wide exploration gets converge-now or cancel
237: immediately; sunk cost is never a reason to let it finish. The parent runs all
238: gates; reviewers never do.
239: **Agent lifecycle (owner decision 2026-09-09):** never end a turn while
240: turn-owned sub-agents are still running: join them first (`agent` wait with
241: `until="all"` per owned id) or detach them deliberately (`detached=true`). A
242: child parked as interrupted is a continuable checkpoint: resume the same lane
243: with `resume_from`, never re-dispatch a fresh agent over it. Re-dispatch is
244: justified only when the base has moved so far that the parked work is
245: worthless — cancel the parked record then, and say so. Terminal records cost
246: nothing to keep; a new wave never starts while the previous one's lanes are
247: still open.
248: **Reviewer budgets are input bounds (owner decision 2026-09-09):** the runtime
249: config sets no per-role step/token budget (only `max_subagents`,
250: `max_concurrent`, model strength), so a "~12 tool calls" limit is prose and
251: will be exceeded. The enforceable guarantee is what the parent puts in front
252: of the child: hand each reviewer per-file diff slices or a file list whose
253: combined diff output is small — never a directory-level diff. Tool output is
254: capped; a truncated diff gets re-read and re-run, which is what burns
255: hundreds of k tokens. A reviewer whose output was truncated narrows with
256: `read_file`/single grep — it never re-issues the same wide command.
257: **Claims, docs and parallel writers (owner decision 2026-09-10):** a comment, an ADR sentence and a FEATURES bullet are **claims about
258: the code**. Three rules follow, and they bind parent and child alike.
259: 
260: 1. **Write only what you have read.** A docs/ADR writer dispatched beside code
261:    writers describes the code that is **in the tree**, verified by reading it —
262:    never the work in flight. If the code has not landed, the docs writer either
263:    waits for it or writes nothing about it; an ADR that records a decision the
264:    tree does not implement is a false claim on the most authoritative document
265:    in the repo. Prefer dispatching the docs pass **after** the code pass, and
266:    have the parent re-check the ADR against the diff before committing.
267: 2. **A change that makes a claim false fixes the claim in the same diff.** Grep
268:    for the sentence you just invalidated (the old behaviour often survives in a
269:    sibling file's comment, a test comment or the ADR) and correct it there and
270:    then. This is the recurring defect of this repo: code that is right beside
271:    prose that is not.
272: 3. **One writer per file, and expect the checkout to be shared.** Parallel
273:    writers get disjoint `write_roots`; a child whose role is read-only or
274:    docs-only may lose `bash` entirely while a peer writes in the same checkout
275:    (`Tool bash cannot prove a bounded file target …`). That is not a failure to
276:    retry: instruct such children to verify by `read`/`edit` and to say what they
277:    could not run, and keep **all gates in the parent**.
278: 
279: **Invariant tests (owner decision 2026-09-10):** a mechanism the ADR names has at
280: least one test that **fails when the mechanism is removed** — not a test that
281: the code merely runs. The list is not decorative: it is how "we implemented X"
282: stays true a month later. When a review names a mechanism as untested (claim
283: epoch and fencing, the `missed` entry, two agents racing one claim, the
284: recovery of an abandoned run, the per-action ledger, an unreadable document),
285: the fix includes the test. A mock that stands in for a server behaviour the code
286: depends on pins that assumption with a test **next to the simulation**, and the
287: live probe it owes stays written down as owed. Reordering effects against their
288: intent line (or the reverse) means running the affected area's tests before
289: claiming the reorder is safe — that reorder is exactly what a stored document
290: has to keep agreeing with.
291: 
292: **Every review ends with the owner's decisions (owner decision 2026-09-09):**
293: the fixed deliverable is numbered findings (BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR/NIT) with
294: file:line evidence, a five-line summary, a VERDICT, and a closing **"Open
295: decisions for the owner"** section mapping each actionable finding to a
296: concrete choice with a recommendation. The parent forwards that section
297: verbatim; findings without a decision line are how reviews stopped being
298: actionable.
299: **Rules layering (owner decision 2026-09-09):** rules that must bind
300: dispatched sub-agents live, self-contained, in this file — children load the
301: repo's project instructions and nothing else. Owner-global counterparts live
302: in global memory and are labelled "(global user rule, active here)" when
303: mirrored here. Change the global entry first, then mirror; never keep a third
304: copy (skills and dispatch prompts restate the recipe by reference only).
305: **Merge/edit hygiene (owner decision 2026-09-09):** when resolving a conflict with the edit tool, the
306: oldText span must include the full `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` marker lines
307: — never start below the opening marker; when taking a whole side wholesale,
308: strip markers with sed in the same command. No file is staged or committed
309: until a marker grep on that file (`<<<<<<<`, `>>>>>>>`, `^=======$`) returns
310: zero in the same shell invocation. Verification is per write step, never
311: batched at the end of a long run. Whole-tree rename scans (e.g. for
312: `ihasmail`) are never truncated with head/tail — scan per file with bounded
313: output instead.
314: **Every push is gated** (`npm run check:ci`: typecheck + Biome lint + the check
315: scripts + tests + build); the `.githooks/pre-push` hook enforces it, enabled per
316: clone with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. The hook gates the tree being
317: pushed: it reads the ref updates git hands it, refuses a push whose tip is not
318: the checked-out commit (this hook can only verify the checkout it runs in), and
319: keys the cache on the pushed commit's tree. The hook is checkpoint-driven:
320: the default runs the full gate; `GATE=fast` runs only typecheck+lint; `GATE=off`
321: skips deliberately. It also skips when every changed path is binary and named by
322: no check, or when the exact tree already passed in that mode
323: (cache `.git/gate-cache`). Bypass a single push with `--no-verify`. `ci.yml` does
324: not run on push: it is the release pre-check, and only Dependabot's pull requests
325: start it, because their branches never pass through the local hook.
326: 
327: **An action's `uses:` names a full commit SHA**, with the version it is in a
328: comment beside it (owner decision 2026-09-23): a tag is a moving target, and
329: one that is repointed runs in this repository's release path with its token.
330: A `./.github/workflows/…` reference is a workflow here rather than an action,
331: and is not pinned. Dependabot's `github-actions` updates are what move these —
332: a bump that moves the SHA without the version comment beside it is a review
333: finding. `npm run workflow:pin` is the check that enforces both: an action
334: named by a tag, or pinned with no version beside it, fails the gate. It reads
335: the same files for the two values a workflow cannot import — the Node line and
336: the image the pruner targets — and asserts the first against `engines.node` and
337: the second against the published `IMAGE`, so a Node move or a rename is one
338: edit. The workflows this repository owns are ours; upstream's CI is not taken.
339: 
340: **CodeQL runs with the release, on GitHub only** (ADR 0023, owner decisions
341: 2026-09-27 and 2026-10-18): the analysis is `.github/workflows/codeql.yml`,
342: called by `release.yml` as a pre-check — `cut` waits on it — and run weekly and
343: on dispatch besides. It is not a per-push gate, and there is **no local
344: analysis**: no script, no bundled toolchain, no `CODEQL_CLI` lookup. A finding
345: the hosted run prints is work to do in the same change, like any other finding a
346: gate prints.
347: **Static analysis and secret scanning run on every push and pull request, and
348: once a night** (ADR 0022): `.github/workflows/ci-security.yml` runs Semgrep at
349: ERROR level across the TypeScript, Node, security-audit and OWASP rule packs,
350: and Gitleaks over the history through the official action pinned to a commit.
351: Neither is in `check:ci` — Semgrep is a second toolchain and Gitleaks wants the
352: whole history — and a finding either prints is work to do in the same change.
353: The identifiers Gitleaks is told are not secrets live in `.gitleaks.toml`, each
354: a positive proof rather than a silence, and `.semgrepignore` points the SAST
355: scan at the code that ships — test files reach the local mock over http and
356: carry fixtures, so the packs' HTTP patterns fire on them by construction.
357: **Coding first, the review beside it, the gate at the push (owner decision
358: 2026-10-14):** a task that carries a plan of several units does **all** of its
359: work — coding, docs and the claim fixes that go with them — landing one commit
360: per finished unit, and runs **no check at all**: no typecheck, no Biome, no
361: check script, no test, no build, neither between units nor at the end of the
362: turn. With several changes in flight those runs cost more time and machine than
363: the work they judge, and a run started before the next unit lands is already
364: stale when it finishes. What passes over the work is the **review** — small,
365: bounded, read-only readers by area, their findings fixed in the change — and a
366: dispatched child runs no gate either. The gate runs **once, before a push**,
367: which is where it belongs: `npm run check:ci` through the `.githooks/pre-push`
368: hook, and a push that has not passed it does not happen. `check:ci` is a series of
369: scripts; `npm run prepush` is that series under the name the hook calls, and
370: `prepush:full` is an alias of `check:ci` for muscle memory. The owner decides when a push is made; **0/0/0** is
371: the standard of that one gate, not of every step along the way.
372: **Commit is automatic; push is not (owner decision 2026-09-24).** Every finished
373: unit is committed on its own, with no per-turn request (the rule above). A push
374: still needs the owner to say push in the current turn.
375: **The feature inventory stays current.** `FEATURES.md` is the inventory of
376: what Gilbert does (its upstream text arrives by merge, renamed); every
377: feature Gilbert implements beyond upstream is written there, in the same
378: change that implements it, and updated whenever later work changes it. An
379: upstream merge is not done when it compiles — it is done when the merged
380: delta has been rebranded (gilbert-upstream-rebrand) **and** the inventory
381: has been reconciled: features the merge adds/removes/changes are reflected
382: in `FEATURES.md`, and the Gilbert-added sections survive intact. ADRs record
383: the decisions behind features; the inventory records the features.
384: **A merge takes a change, not a file — and a collision is decided, not
385: assumed.** Where the tree diverged on purpose, an upstream hunk applied
386: verbatim undoes a decision nobody re-opened — silently, since it neither
387: conflicts nor fails a test. What is forbidden is the silence, not the
388: direction: read both sides, take the better one, and rewrite the ADR or
389: comment in the same change — including when upstream's version is the better
390: one, which it often is. Two deliberate designs that both work are the user's
391: choice, not the merge's. Recipe: `gilbert-upstream-rebrand`.
392: **The public docs lead with Gilbert's own.** `README.md` and `FEATURES.md`
393: open with what this project owns — groups, chat, and above all the agents,
394: whose section is the detailed one — and treat the upstream client as a
395: pointer: a line saying it is upstream's and where its documentation lives,
396: with its detail kept afterwards for completeness and never as the lead. A
397: change that makes a sentence in any public doc false fixes it in the same
398: commit, and a new Gilbert feature is written where the reader starts, not
399: only in the section that happens to own it.
400: `origin/main` carries **branch protection** (private repo, set through the
401: API): it refuses a force push and a branch deletion, with `enforce_admins` off
402: so the owner can still bypass it — the point is to guard the two pushes that
403: cannot be undone, not to bind the owner. Nothing else is required of it: no
404: review, no status check, since the gate a push meets is the local pre-push hook
405: — so direct commit + push to main is still the normal flow. Lifting or widening
406: the protection is the owner's call, never a side effect of another change; when
407: it moves, this sentence and `CONTRIBUTING.md` are what state it.
408: **A Dependabot pull request merges itself once the CI is green, and only
409: then.** `dependabot-auto-merge.yml` triggers on the CI run's completion rather
410: than on the pull request — which is also what lets its token write, since the
411: read-only restriction applies to workflows Dependabot triggers directly — and
412: merges the commit the CI verified (`--match-head-commit`). A major update, or
413: one the workflow cannot classify, waits for a person.
414: **Releases are called manually by the user — for now there are none and none are
415: automated.** Never tag, publish, or trigger release/publish workflows on your
416: own (see `.github/workflows/release.yml`, `publish.yml`). The procedure, what a
417: release verifies and how it is rolled back are `docs/releasing.md`.
418: **Upstream is download-only (ADR 0002):** upstream releases are fetched
419: directly by the merge that takes them in (ADR 0002) — there is no mirror
420: branch — and the mail core merges them in. Nothing flows the other way — no contributions, no PRs, no upstream-shaped
421: fork. Common work stays here, renamed or not.
422: **Excluded upstream files (never absorbed; Gilbert's version always wins):**
423: upstream `CLAUDE.md` and `.github/FUNDING.yml` (owner decision 2026-09-06).
424: `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md` and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` are upstream's
425: process and contacts — ask before changing or acting on them.
426: 
427: Full law: load `.opencode/skills/gilbert-project/SKILL.md`. Renames: load
428: `.opencode/skills/gilbert-branding/SKILL.md`. UI strings & languages: load
429: `.opencode/skills/gilbert-i18n/SKILL.md`. Settings & policy: load
430: `.opencode/skills/gilbert-settings/SKILL.md`. Group-owned data & features: load
431: `.opencode/skills/gilbert-groups/SKILL.md`. Global contacts: load
432: `.opencode/skills/gilbert-global-contacts/SKILL.md`. Stalwart internals, quirks &
433: integration: load `.opencode/skills/gilbert-stalwart/SKILL.md`. Upstream merges:
434: load `.opencode/skills/gilbert-upstream-rebrand/SKILL.md`. Controls, empty
435: states, counters, icons and whether two screens look alike: load
436: `.opencode/skills/gilbert-ui/SKILL.md`. The skill that governs
437: a kind of work is loaded before the first edit of it.
438: 
439: ## Automatic by default (global user rule, active here)
440: 
441: - **If the product needs something, make it happen** — do not add a button, a
442:   wizard or a setup step that asks the reader to do it by hand. A control is
443:   added only where the owner genuinely must choose; everything else is the
444:   behaviour that just works.
445: - **No per-user complexity.** A thing that serves everyone is set up once by the
446:   product, not configured again for each person.
447: - **User-friendly by default, without weakening security.** The automatic path
448:   keeps the same door, the same permissions and the same boundaries: it removes
449:   steps, not checks.
450: - Before proposing a control, ask what should happen with nobody watching and
451:   make that the behaviour.
452: - **A tool the work needs, the agent installs.** A check, a validator, a build
453:   dependency: when the task needs it and installing it is not destructive, it is
454:   installed and used — never asked for, never worked around. Asking is for an
455:   action that changes or destroys something the owner owns, not for acquiring a
456:   tool the work in hand already requires. The global entry is canonical; this
457:   mirrors it.
458: 
459: ## Shell: nothing unbounded in the foreground (global user rule, active here)
460: 
461: - A command that is not bounded to a few seconds goes to the background at
462:   launch (`background=true` / `task_shell_start`) and is polled. The runtime's
463:   own tool text puts the line at >5 s; there is no global default and no
464:   auto-promotion, and `Ctrl+B → /jobs` is the owner's manual override, never
465:   the recovery path for a command an agent launched.
466: - **A timeout is sized to the work, never to a default maximum** (global user
467:   rule, active here): a command that normally returns in a second gets a few
468:   seconds, not minutes. Tool calls stop being handed a long timeout "to be
469:   safe" — a long timeout does not make a stale command finish, and is no
470:   substitute for knowing the work is done.
471: - **Throw it into the background and poll, rather than waiting a timeout out**
472:   (global user rule, active here): a command that is stale or hung is killed
473:   or backgrounded and polled — sitting through its timeout is lost time, and
474:   the owner must never be the one who waits it out for the agent.
475: - If a foreground command is already sitting with no output, move it to `/jobs`
476:   yourself and poll it, or kill it and relaunch it in the background — the
477:   owner must never be the one who unsticks it.
478: 
479: ## Worktrees
480: 
481: - A worktree of this repository lives in `.worktree/` — the canonical name, here
482:   and in every repository: `<repo>/.worktree/<slug>`. Not `.worktrees/`, not
483:   `<name>.worktree/`, no per-tool spelling.
484: - Create one with `git worktree add .worktree/<slug>`.
485: - A worktree is a checkout, not content. `/.worktree/` is ignored — in a
486:   repository whose `.gitignore` belongs to upstream, the pattern lives in
487:   `.git/info/exclude` instead — so `git add -A` can never stage one.

<skill_content name="gilbert-project">
# Skill: gilbert-project

# Gilbert — project law

## 1. Identity

- The project is **Gilbert**, a backronym for **G**eneral-purpose **I**ntelligent **L**ifecycle **B**utler for **E**nterprise **R**esource **T**raceability. The canonical statement lives at the top of `README.md`; keep this skill and that file in sync.
- Gilbert is its own product, of which the mail client is one part. The mail
  client is based on Coffey Labs' **ihasmail** — the attribution, with its
  address, is in `NOTICE` — and remote `upstream` is no_push, `origin` is
  `sequico/gilbert`. Upstream is
  download-only (ADR 0002): releases are fetched directly by the merge that
  takes them in (ADR 0002) and the mail core merges them in, and nothing is
  contributed back.
  Ask before inventing product behaviour the acronym implies but
  the code does not have.
- **Snapshot mode**: files and comments describe the code as it is now; never
  narrate a rename or a migration — history lives in git. **Documents are
  edited in place too**, ADRs included: what a record describes changing means
  the record is rewritten in the same change, never superseded by a second one
  and never left narrating the version it replaced.
- Licence AGPL-3.0-or-later; `LICENSE` and `NOTICE` keep Coffey Labs' copyright (the mail core is their derivative work). Do not strip attribution.

## 2. Naming rule (the one that keeps every doc coherent)

- **Prose** about the product says "Gilbert".
- **Every code and build identifier is `gilbert`** — docs must match:
  `APP_NAME`
  default "Gilbert", package names `gilbert`/`@gilbert/*`, `GILBERT_VERSION`
  build arg, `X-Requested-With: gilbert`, the visible shell
  (title/manifest/login copy) and every product-naming UI string and catalog
  key, the app folder, the sieve script name, storage keys, MIME types, the
  `[gilbert]` log prefix and the `session.gilbert` extension. Full list:
  `gilbert-branding`.
- **`ihasmail` remains only where upstream's real name must stay**: the AGPL
  attribution in `LICENSE`/`NOTICE` — `NOTICE` being the only file that carries
  its addresses (ihasmail.org, docs.ihasmail.org, demo.ihasmail.com,
  git.coffeylabs.org/coffey-labs/ihasmail, the GitHub-era issues and PRs in
  ihasmail-github-archive) — and the lineage prose in `README`/ADR 0002, which
  names upstream and points at `NOTICE`. **No public doc links to upstream** —
  not `README`, `FEATURES.md`, `KNOWN-ISSUES.md`, `ROADMAP.md` or an ADR — and
  a sentence that carried such a link is rewritten to stand without it. Never
  rename or unpresent the attribution itself.

## 3. Architecture law

- JMAP only, to Stalwart. No IMAP/POP3/SMTP fallback and no database of its own: everything durable lives in Stalwart; the container is disposable; with `IMMUTABLE=1` there is no writable filesystem, and nothing Gilbert keeps durably is on it anyway (sessions included).
- **The installation's configuration is one document in Stalwart** (ADR 0009): `installation.json` in the Master account's own `gilbert` app folder, read whole at boot (`bootstrap.ts` → `config.ts`'s `useConfiguration`), created on the first boot with the defaults and a generated app secret, and edited at Administration → Installation. The environment carries the handshake, the container's own facts, the image's facts and the operator's own switch — and nothing that the document decides for a booted process. `BASE_PATH` is the image's fact rather than a document field (the build argument and the container's copy are the same value), and a production process that states no prefix refuses to serve; a key that must not be the installation's (`BASE_PATH`, `GILBERT_AGENT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_PROVIDER`) is read from the environment and nowhere else — see `.env.example` for the list in a deployment's own words.
- `web/` = React 19 + TypeScript SPA (Vite): `src/jmap` (client/push/types), `src/store` (zustand: session, mail, compose, contacts, calendar, files, sieve, settings, mdn, scheduled), `src/lib` (incl. `src/lib/smime`: pure-TS S/MIME verification over WebCrypto), `src/views`, `src/ui`, `src/locales`. `server/` = Node + Hono proxy (`/api/jmap`, blob, upload, EventSource, image, ics) — responses compressed, the data path per-session rate-limited (`apiRateLimited`), with an optional `rawPushRelay` — and an in-memory mock Stalwart in `server/src/mock` (which serves really-signed S/MIME fixtures from `signedMessages.ts`).
- Standing values: graceful degradation per JMAP capability; fail loudly rather than quietly; sanitised HTML with remote images blocked; strict CSP; settings follow the account (`settings.json` in the account's Files) with localStorage only as a cache.
- **A client-side rule is asked from one module and guarded on the effect** (ADR 0013). The mail deletion rule is the worked example: `web/src/lib/mailDelete.ts` is the only place that answers what a delete does and who may take one, `store/mail/` asks it inside `destroy`, `emptyMailbox` and `destroyMailbox` — never only in the menu that draws the entry — and it answers **codes**, with the sentence composed where it is shown so a catalogue can translate it. It refuses every account that is not provably the reader's own (`isOwnMailAccount`), not "a group by the classifier": the group classifier answers nothing until the account probe has landed, so asking it would fail open in the window a boot sits in. The rule is a convention the client keeps and never a boundary — say so wherever it is described.
- The mock reproduces real-server quirks on purpose (per-account `urn:stalwart:jmap`, 2047-byte signatures, Stalwart's calendar vocabulary, renumbering synthetic ids). Where mock and server disagree, ask a real server.

## 4. Toolchain and gates

- Node on the latest LTS line (24 today — the Dockerfile, CI, engines and @types/node all say the same one), npm workspaces. `npm install` once.
- `npm run dev` (real Stalwart) · `npm run dev:mock` (demo@example.com / demo, mock on :8788) · `npm run dev:mock:no-future-release` · `npm run dev:mock:no-keyword-sort` · `npm run typecheck` · `npm test` (vitest for web, node:test for server) · `npm run build` · `npm start` · `npm run prepush:full` (alias of `check:ci`).
- i18n: `npm run i18n:coverage`, `npm run i18n:check`; catalogs in `web/src/locales/*.ts`.
- Lint + format: **Biome** (`biome.jsonc`) via `npm run lint` / `npm run lint:fix`; part of `prepush` and of the CI release pre-check. The config is calibrated to this repo's measured style and its off-rules are deliberate and commented — never re-enable a disabled rule just to silence a file; adjust the code or argue the rule.
- **CodeQL runs with the release, on GitHub only** (ADR 0023): `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` is called by `release.yml` as a pre-check (nothing is cut on an unclean analysis) and runs weekly and on demand besides; it is deliberately not in the per-push gate. There is **no local analysis and no local toolchain** — no script, no `CODEQL_CLI`, no database built in a checkout. A finding the hosted run prints is work to do in the same change, like any other finding a gate prints.
- Version comes from git at build time: `node scripts/version.mjs`; nothing writes a version into the tree.
- Done means: typecheck passes, the relevant tests pass, the diff has been read, and claims are verified against tests or a live server — not exit codes alone.
- Code comments, documentation and every commit message are written in **English** (repo-wide rule set by the owner). Chat replies follow the user's language — the chat is not repo content.

## 4b. Claims, documents and tests

A comment, an ADR sentence and a `FEATURES.md` bullet are **claims about the
code**, and this repo's recurring defect is a true sentence standing beside
code that stopped matching it. Three habits keep the two together:

- **Write only what you read.** Documentation written beside code that is still
  being written — by a peer agent or by you — describes the tree, never the
  work in flight. Verify the line you are describing; if it is not there yet,
  either wait or say nothing about it.
- **A change that falsifies a claim fixes the claim in the same diff.** Grep the
  sentence you just invalidated: the old behaviour usually survives in another
  file, a test's comment or an ADR. Every record is edited in place — `Proposed`
  and `Accepted` alike — so an ADR always states the decision as it stands and
  git holds the version before it. A number is minted for a decision that is
  new, or where the owner asks for one explicitly.
- **Every mechanism the ADR names has a test that fails if the mechanism is
  removed.** A test that only shows the code runs proves nothing about the
  guarantee. When a review names something as untested, the fix includes the
  test. A mock standing in for a server behaviour pins that assumption with a
  test next to the simulation, and the live probe it owes is written down as
  owed (see `gilbert-stalwart`).
- Reordering an effect against its intent line is a change to what a stored
  document means: run that area's tests before calling it safe.

Parallel writers (fleet work): one writer per file, disjoint `write_roots`, and
expect a peer's writes in the same checkout to cost a read-only child its
`bash` — that child verifies by reading and says what it could not run, and
**every gate stays in the parent**.

Companion skills: string/i18n work loads `gilbert-i18n`; anything settings- or policy-shaped loads `gilbert-settings`; Global contacts loads `gilbert-global-contacts`.

## 3b. The agent vocabulary and what the agent is

- **Three words, and they are not synonyms.** One **Master** is the principal
everything belongs to: the account in Stalwart (`gilbert@…`), its address, its
password, its grants and the model it uses. Its **agent** is the process that
acts as it, and it runs inside `gilbertserver`. An unqualified **"worker"** means
the browser's service worker and nothing else.
- **The agent's decisions are seven records, and the tree carries them.**
**ADR 0027** (a described catalogue of tools, and one model per installation
chosen in Administration), **0028** (what it decides and what only a person
decides, an override being an administrator's and proved by the directory),
**0029** (one conversation in chat and mail, in words), **0030** (a run is a
document, and the record is the product), **0031** (a group's engagement is a
rule in prose, written by an administrator), **0032** (one installation claims
its agent) and **0033** (its memory is a graph of facts it recalls). Each record's `Implementation` line says what
the tree carries and what it still owes, and it is the truth about the tree
rather than a summary of the design: read it instead of assuming. The
catalogue and its authority guard are `server/src/agent/tools.ts`, a rule is
`server/src/agent/rule.ts`, the model's turns are `server/src/agent/model.ts`,
and the loop that works a run is `server/src/agent/loop.ts`, which the server's
own boot starts with itself (`server/src/agent/supervisor.ts`, a pass every ten
seconds over the groups the Master holds, read from the mail server on each
pass). **The mail channel is in the tree**: `mail.ask` parks a run on a person by
mail, `mailAnsweredBy` continues it on the thread, `mail.send` goes outward on a
person's word or a rule's own declaration, and `personWord` (`agent/trust.ts`) is
what decides whether a message is anybody's word at all — a submission on the
account the server authenticated, and never an outside verdict until its
`authserv-id` is probed.
- **Identifiers follow those words.** Two halves: the names, and the things that
are contracts rather than names — a field in a document an installation has
already written, a refusal code a client composes a sentence from, an environment
variable an operator set. A contract moves with every reader and writer of it in
one change, or it does not move at all: `GILBERT_AGENT_*` is the Master's
handshake and the operators' spelling, and it stays.

## 5. Change workflow

- Read `README.md` and the affected area before editing; smallest coherent diff; report adjacent issues rather than silently expanding scope.
- Commit is automatic: each finished unit lands on its own, with no per-turn
  request (owner decision 2026-09-24). A push still needs the owner to say it in
  the current turn.
- **Releases are manual.** The user calls releases by hand; for now there are none and none are automated. Never tag, create a release, or trigger the upstream release/publish workflows (`.github/workflows/release.yml`, `publish.yml`) on your own.
- `SECURITY.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` are Gilbert's own: the process they describe and the contact they name (`info@sequi.company`) are this project's, and upstream's attribution stays in `NOTICE`. Ask the user before changing the process they describe.
- A deep rename diverges from upstream and complicates every future sync — state that cost before doing one (see `gilbert-branding`).
- **Upstream is download-only (ADR 0002).** Upstream releases are fetched
  directly by the merge that takes them in (ADR 0002) — there is no mirror
  branch — and the mail core merges them in. Nothing flows back — no PRs to
  coffey-labs/ihasmail, no upstream-shaped
  fork, no un-renaming. The sync direction stays upstream → main.
- Syncing upstream: upstream's locale catalogs are a key-superset of Gilbert's trimmed ones and more complete — when catalog files conflict, adopt the upstream catalog wholesale rather than merging entries, then run `npm run i18n:check`. Upstream's `CLAUDE.md` and `.github/FUNDING.yml` stay excluded (owner decision); monitor `CLAUDE.md` for agent guidance worth porting into this file or the skills.

<skill_content name="gilbert-upstream-rebrand">
# Skill: gilbert-upstream-rebrand

# Gilbert — taking in an upstream merge

Two things are checked in one pass, and neither is the other's job:

1. **The naming law** — every `ihasmail` the delta introduces is renamed to
   `gilbert`/`Gilbert`, except the upstream mentions that must stay.
2. **The collisions** — where upstream's change lands on ground our tree already
   decided, someone has to *choose*, with both versions in view. Which side wins
   is the outcome of that reading, not a rule: upstream is often right, and its
   version may well be the better one. What this forbids is neither side — it is
   the change that happens **without anyone choosing it**.

## When this applies

Upstream releases are fetched directly by the merge that takes them into
`main` (ADR 0002), and a daily watch reports a release main has not taken in.
That report is a pointer rather than a verdict: a hand-take never makes the
release's own commit an ancestor, so `docs/upstream.md` — one row per upstream
commit and what became of it — is what settles whether a commit is already in.
Upstream code is written for ihasmail: it ships `ihasmail` identifiers,
`[ihasmail]` log prefixes, `ihasmail-…` device/header strings, ihasmail.example
fixtures and prose that calls the product ihasmail. Gilbert's naming law
(gilbert-branding) forbids all of that except the upstream/AGPL mentions. The
mail core is based on ihasmail, not named after it.

The second hazard is not about naming at all and is the more expensive one.
Upstream moves fast and its decisions are usually reasoned ones — it is the
larger project, it sees the real deployments, and a security pass there is worth
taking seriously. But Gilbert's tree has also diverged on purpose, and a commit
touching such a spot carries *its* version of it. Applied verbatim, that hunk is
a choice nobody made: our decision is gone, and the only trace is an ADR, a key
or a comment that is now false. It does not conflict, it does not fail a test,
and it arrives looking like upstream tidying.

So the job is not to defend our version. It is to turn each collision into a
decision — read both sides, judge them on their merits, take the better one, and
leave the record saying what was chosen and why. Upstream winning is a normal
outcome; the ADR is then rewritten in the same change, because we are
*deliberately* changing our decision.

A merge of upstream code is therefore **not done** when conflicts are resolved
and tests pass. It is done when the merged delta has been rebranded **and** every
hunk that landed on ground we had already decided flatly has been chosen rather
than inherited. This skill is that checklist.

## Rules of thumb

- **A merge takes a change, not a file — and a collision is a fork in the road,
  not a verdict.** Before accepting an upstream hunk, read what our tree already
  decided in that spot, and what the upstream change was actually *for*. Then
  pick, on merit: our version, theirs, or one built from both — which is often
  the honest answer, and is what happened to the body cap (`loginBody` below):
  take the new bound upstream introduced, keep the tighter number we had already
  chosen for sign-in.
- **What is refused is the silent application, not the direction.** Holding our
  side out of habit is as much a failure as taking theirs out of habit: a tree
  that never absorbs a better idea from upstream is not being careful, it is
  calcifying. An upstream fix that is simply better — a real bug we also have, a
  simpler shape, a fact about Stalwart we got wrong — is taken, and our ADR and
  our comment are corrected in the same commit.
- **An upstream hunk that falsifies a claim in our tree is a decision, not a
  cleanup.** If the hunk would make an ADR sentence, a `FEATURES.md` bullet or a
  comment false, that is the signal to stop and read both sides: either our
  version stays where it is, or we are changing our decision and the claim is
  rewritten in the same change to say what the code now does. Silence is the one
  option that is not on the table — landing the hunk and leaving the claim
  standing is the defect this rule exists to prevent (repo rule: *a change that
  makes a claim false fixes the claim in the same diff*,
  `.opencode/skills/gilbert-upstream-rebrand/SKILL.md`).
- **Some collisions are the owner's call — but read them before escalating
  them.** Two deliberate designs that both work, ours and theirs, are not
  something to settle inside a merge: name both, say what each costs, and put the
  choice to the user. That is the last resort rather than the first, though,
  because a collision read only from our side *looks* like taste. Reading what
  upstream's change was for, and what our own code was actually doing, is what
  turns most of them into a defect, a fact, or a synthesis — the push
  subscription below was escalated first as two designs and turned out to hold a
  bug of ours, an upstream fact we were wrong about, and one genuine collision.
  A merge is still the wrong place to redesign a feature, in either direction.
- **Prefer taking a delta to merging the release.** When the change we want sits
  in a handful of upstream commits and the merge would drag in hundreds of files
  we have diverged from, hand-take it (the way `84dea39` took four fixes out of
  `v2026.9.15-pr369` rather than merging 227 files). A hand-take is where this
  rule is easiest to obey: each hunk is read on its own, against ours.
- Excluded upstream files (CLAUDE.md, .github/FUNDING.yml, …) stay at
  Gilbert's version, never absorbed: rule and ask-first list live in
  `.opencode/skills/gilbert-upstream-rebrand/SKILL.md` (Upstream section) — read it before merging.
- Rename the delta, not the repo. Only files the merge touched need a look:
  new upstream files, files whose upstream hunks added strings, and tests
  that assert on them. `git diff <merge-base>..HEAD --stat` bounds it.
- `ihasmail` may stay only where upstream's real name must stay: AGPL lineage
  in `README`/`LICENSE`/`NOTICE`/ADR 0002, and upstream-owned legal lines
  ("If you run a modified ihasmail…"). Upstream's addresses
  (ihasmail.org, docs.ihasmail.org, demo.ihasmail.com,
  git.coffeylabs.org/coffey-labs/ihasmail, the GitHub-era issues and PRs in
  ihasmail-github-archive) live in `NOTICE` and nowhere else: a merged doc hunk
  that links to one arrives as prose naming upstream, or as a plain issue
  number, with the reader sent to `NOTICE` for the address.
- Everything else says `gilbert`/`Gilbert`: prose about the product says
  "Gilbert"; identifiers are lowercase `gilbert`.
- Snapshot mode: comments describe the merged code as it is, never
  "upstream says X but here Y". Do not narrate the rename in a comment.
- Keep upstream behaviour identical *as far as the change goes*: the rename
  pass is not a review pass. Real changes are the collisions above, decided on
  purpose — not a licence to "improve" upstream code on the way through.
- Renames are automatic and never a question: any `ihasmail` the delta
  introduces outside the stay-list above is renamed during the merge —
  including user-visible identifiers such as a shipped theme or palette id.
  Judgment applies only to the stay-list, never to the user.

## Worked collisions

Four real ones, from the `v2026.9.15-pr369` → `v2026.9.18` range. Read them as
*how the call was made*, not as precedents — and note that they went four
different ways: one is a bound taken from upstream with our tighter number kept
on top, one ends the other way with the record rewritten, one is settled by the
one-source-of-truth rule rather than by preference, and one took upstream's
diagnosis, kept our design and turned up a defect on our own side. None of them
is "upstream was wrong"; in every one, upstream's change was worth taking and
the question was only what it was worth taking *over*. Where upstream is simply
right — and often it is, being the larger project with the real deployments in
front of it — the reading ends that way, and the ADR, the inventory bullet or
the comment changes with it.

- **`loginBody`: a third version, built from both.** We cap sign-in at 16 KiB
  (`d45f011`) — the one endpoint that reads a body from somebody not yet signed
  in — and scope limits by name (`/account/*`, `/admin/*`). Upstream caps every
  JSON route at 64 KiB and exempts the data path by pattern. Neither side's
  file is taken: the *change* is (a bound on every JSON route, an exemption
  shaped like the route), and our tighter number and clearer scoping stay on top
  of it. Reconciling is not always choosing.
- **`ApiKey` went upstream's way, and the record moved with it.** Upstream's
  security pass (`dfe885a`) removes the object from the self-service allowlist
  while adding the real fix — a refusal of every `x:` `set` — and this tree had
  copied the list from upstream's own draft, so `ApiKey` was never a decision
  here, only an inheritance. Two things settled it: upstream is the side that
  re-thought it, and no surface in Gilbert mints or shows an API key, so an
  entry for it was reach nobody had asked for. It came off the list, ADR 0015's
  sentence lost the name and gained the reason, and `adminGate.test.ts` now
  asserts the refusal. **This is the shape a collision takes when upstream is
  right**: the change is taken and the claim that named the old behaviour is
  rewritten in the same commit.
- **`staleBuild`: a duplicate module, which is not a matter of taste.** We have
  `web/src/lib/staleBuild.ts`; upstream has `web/src/lib/sw/staleBuild.ts`, and
  its `sw/` changes (#394–#396) touch theirs. This one is decided by the
  one-source-of-truth rule rather than by preference: two implementations of one
  behaviour is a defect whatever upstream says. Two further things in the same
  hunk are not judgement calls at all — the storage key reverting to
  `ihasmail:reloaded-for` from `gilbert:reloaded-for` (naming law), and a
  comment stating that **a deploy signs everyone out because an immutable
  instance holds sessions in memory**, which is false here, where sessions live
  in the account's own document (ADR 0001). Reconcile by taking the *behaviour*
  into our file; never by landing their module beside ours.
- **The push subscription: upstream's diagnosis won, our design was kept, and
  the third thing was ours to fix.** ADR 0014 owns this surface. At the time of
  the merge it said `types: ["Email"]` and planned `["Email", "FileNode"]` so a
  group's chat would wake the device; upstream's `4054f82` subscribes to
  `EmailDelivery` instead, and that is a better answer to the question the type
  list was there for — a delivery is the only thing worth waking a closed client
  for, and `Email` changes on every read and move from any client. So the type
  list moved to upstream's, and the *plan* was not dropped but deferred: naming
  `FileNode` before the worker can read what changed would render a chat write as
  "New mail", so the chat wake-up stays owed on the record with the reason
  written down.

  Three findings in that one collision, of three different kinds, which is why
  it is worth reading as a case rather than as a precedent:

  1. a fact upstream was simply right about, where the record changed with the
     code (`EmailDelivery`);
  2. a decision of ours that upstream had not made, where a first reading said
     "the owner's call" and a second one — reading what each subscription
     actually consumes — showed the loudest symptom was a bug we shared, not two
     designs to choose between (the payload asked for no `id`, so the Archive
     and Mark-read buttons the worker draws could never appear);
  3. a genuine collision, neither side's to settle alone: gilbertserver told a
     browser's row from its own by the types it asked for, so *changing* that
     type list turned a browser's registration into a candidate for deletion on
     a full quota. Both sides now decide it by the shape of the device id, in
     `server/src/shared/push.ts`, which both tiers already import.

  The lesson worth keeping: **a collision read only from our side looks like a
  matter of taste.** Reading what upstream's change was *for* — and what our own
  code was actually doing — is what turned two of these three from an opinion
  into a defect. Enumerate the collisions, then read them.

**The pattern**, and the reason this list exists: a hunk is hardest to judge
exactly when *both* sides are deliberate. `grep` the ADR index and
`FEATURES.md` for the surface it touches *before* deciding — a record naming the
symbol usually settles it, and a record naming the *other* design means you have
found a question for the user rather than a fix to apply.

## Checklist — run this before committing the merge

1. **List the collisions, before applying anything.** For every file the merge
   touches, compare the two sides of the change:
   `git diff <merge-base>..<upstream-ref> -- <file>` against
   `git diff <merge-base>..HEAD -- <file>`. Where both changed the same region,
   that region is a fork: name it, read both versions *and what each was for*,
   and say which one goes in and why. "Ours" is a defensible answer and so is
   "theirs" — an undeclared one is not. This is the step whose omission is
   invisible in the diff and expensive a month later. Worked cases above.
2. **For every collision, decide and record.** The choices are: take upstream's
   version and rewrite the claim it falsified; keep ours and note why it is
   still better; build the one that takes the change without losing our half;
   or, where both designs are deliberate and working, put it to the user with
   both named and do not land it in the meantime.
3. **Grep the merged delta for `ihasmail`** (case-insensitive). Judge every
   hit against the allowed list above — that judgment is mechanical and never
escalated to the user; do not bulk-replace.
4. **Log prefixes** `[ihasmail]` → `[gilbert]`. These are operator-visible;
   the naming law pins the `[gilbert]` prefix.
5. **Wire and storage identifiers** the client/server exchange or persist:
   `deviceClientId` prefixes, MIME types, storage keys, sieve script names,
   the Web Push device-id prefix and its verification path. `ihasmail-…` →
   `gilbert-…` etc.
6. **Fixture values in tests** (`https://ihasmail.example`, sample
   addresses/URLs that are not the real upstream) → `gilbert.example` or
   equivalent. Real upstream URLs stay.
7. **Prose in comments and docs** describing the product ("the server holds
   a stream to ihasmail") → "Gilbert". Keep mentions of upstream ihasmail
   only when the sentence is about the upstream project itself.
8. **UI strings**: if the merge adds or changes user-visible copy, follow
   gilbert-i18n — keys are English source; add or update catalogue entries
   in every language (de, es, fr, it, ja, nl, pt-BR, ru, uk, zh-Hans) when
   the key is new. A missing key degrades to English by design, but new
   admin/feature copy should ship translated like its neighbours.
9. **App name in copy**: the product's own name appears as the runtime name
   (`APP_NAME`) where possible; where a key embeds "Gilbert", translations
   keep it untranslated.
10. **ADR and claim check**: for every collision, grep the sentence it changes —
   an ADR, a `FEATURES.md` bullet, a comment naming the symbol. Whatever the
   choice was, the sentence says what the code now does in the same change.
   A claim left standing beside code that no longer matches it is the defect,
   whichever side won.
11. **Feature inventory**: a merge is not done when it compiles — reconcile
   `FEATURES.md` with the merged delta (features the merge adds, removes or
   changes are reflected) and make sure the Gilbert-added sections survive
   intact. Repo rule: the inventory stays current on every change and every
   merge (`.opencode/skills/gilbert-upstream-rebrand/SKILL.md`, "The feature inventory stays
   current").

## Verification

- **Every collision has a decision.** Re-read the list from checklist step 1
  against the final diff: each entry says which version went in and why, and no
  entry is there by habit in either direction. An undeclared collision is the
  failure mode this skill exists for — as is a tree that took nothing from
  upstream because "we had already decided".
- **Every claim still true.** For each collision, the ADR / `FEATURES.md` /
  comment that describes it matches the code that landed. Where upstream's
  version won, that sentence was rewritten — and git holds the version before
  it, so nothing needs saying about what it used to be.
- `git diff <merge-base>..HEAD -- server web | grep -i ihasmail` — expect
  only the allowed mentions (or none).
- TypeScript/JSON: `npm run typecheck`.
- Biome: `npm run lint:fix` then `npm run lint` — upstream code arrives
  unformatted; conformance is part of the merge commit.
- Tests: `TZ=UTC npm test` (server and web) — renamed log/device strings
  are often asserted in tests; fix those assertions in the same change.
- UI copy: `npm run i18n:check` — no stale keys, literals quiet.
- Read the final diff once, hunks in order, before committing.

2: 
3: Gilbert's mail core is based on upstream ihasmail, and upstream is
4: **download-only** (ADR 0002): releases are fetched by the merge that takes them
5: in and nothing goes back. `.github/workflows/upstream-watch.yml` asks, once a
6: day, whether the newest release is accounted for: its commit an ancestor of
7: `main`, **or** every work commit it adds carrying a row here. The second
8: question is what a hand-take needs — a hand-take never makes the release's own
9: commit an ancestor, so ancestry alone would report a release whose useful
10: commits were taken one by one as missing forever.
11: 
12: This file is the record that answers it: one row per upstream commit, with what
13: became of it. It is not a mirror and not a second history — the commits are

15: what is already decided is not re-decided.

17: ## The convention that keeps it true

19: A change that takes an upstream **commit** rather than a whole release records
20: the upstream sha in its own message:

23:

26: and the trailers disagree, the trailers are what is true.

---WATCH---
# Say so, once a day, when upstream has cut a release nothing has accounted for.
#
# This repository does not mirror upstream: upstream is fetched directly by the
# merge that takes it in (ADR 0002). What is left to automate is noticing. The
# fetch is cheap and needs no credential, and the only thing this job does with
# what it finds is open an issue a person reads — so it needs no permission
# beyond the ones a workflow is given, and holds nothing that could be stolen
# from a public repository.
#
# A release is accounted for in one of two ways, and the second is what a
# hand-take needs: its own commit is an ancestor of `main` (a merge or a
# wholesale take), or every work commit it adds has a row in `docs/upstream.md`
# — the record that the commit was read and decided, taken or not. Ancestry
# alone calls a hand-take missing forever, since taking commits one by one
# never makes the release's own commit an ancestor.
name: Watch upstream releases

on:
  schedule:
    # Once a day, off the hour. Upstream cuts release tags on merges, so a
    # daily check is well inside their cadence.
    - cron: "17 3 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch: {}

# One watch at a time, so two runs cannot open two issues for one release.
concurrency:
  group: upstream-watch
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  watch:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Find the newest upstream release, and whether main has accounted for it
        id: newest
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git remote add upstream https://git.coffeylabs.org/coffey-labs/ihasmail.git
          # Fetched into their own namespace, never refs/tags: this repository
          # carries its own release tags (v2026.9.5-*), and the two mixed
          # together made the newest-upstream-release check pick one of ours.
          # --prune drops a tag upstream has deleted, so a re-cut one cannot
          # linger; the default branch is fetched to tell a release of this line
          # from a tag cut on a side branch.
          git fetch --prune upstream \
            '+refs/tags/*:refs/upstream/tags/*' \
            '+refs/heads/*:refs/upstream/heads/*'
          main_ref="refs/upstream/heads/main"
          has_main=0
          if git rev-parse --verify -q "$main_ref" >/dev/null; then has_main=1; fi
          # Upstream's release tags are the versioned ones (v2026.9.3-pr272);
          # the v2.16.* and stalwart-* tags are older shapes or branches, not
          # releases. Newest by creation date among those on the default branch,
          # then the one before it: the older release bounds the work the newest
          # one adds. A tag cut on a side branch is not a release of this line.
          candidates=()
          while IFS= read -r ref; do
            [ -n "$ref" ] || continue
            if [ "$has_main" = 1 ] && ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "${ref}^{commit}" "$main_ref"; then
              continue
            fi
            candidates+=("$ref")
          done < <(git for-each-ref --sort=-creatordate --format '%(refname)' 'refs/upstream/tags/v20[0-9][0-9].*')
          newest_full="${candidates[0]:-}"
          if [ -z "$newest_full" ]; then
            echo "No upstream release tag found." >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          prev_full="${candidates[1]:-}"
          tag="${newest_full#refs/upstream/tags/}"
          # Peeled with rev-parse because the tag may be lightweight:
          # for-each-ref's peeled field is only filled for annotated tags, and
          # an empty sha took the merge down with it on 2026-09-06.
          sha="$(git rev-parse "${newest_full}^{commit}")"
          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "sha=$sha" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          # The first question: a release this history has taken in wholesale is
          # one whose commit is an ancestor of main. Nothing is written down to
          # compare against, so nothing can drift out of step with what the
          # history says.
          if git merge-base --is-ancestor "$sha" HEAD; then
            echo "new=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            exit 0
          fi
          # No previous release to bound the range: nothing says what this
          # release adds, so report it rather than guess.
          if [ -z "$prev_full" ]; then
            echo "new=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            exit 0
          fi
          prev_sha="$(git rev-parse "${prev_full}^{commit}")"
          # The previous release must bound this one. If it is not an ancestor
          # of it, `prev..newest` is not "what this release adds" — fail toward
          # the alarm rather than compute a wrong set of commits.
          if ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "$prev_sha" "$sha"; then
            echo "Previous release ${prev_full#refs/upstream/tags/} is not an ancestor of ${tag}: reporting it unaccounted." >&2
            echo "new=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            exit 0
          fi
          # The second question, and the one a hand-take needs: every work
          # commit the release adds has a row in docs/upstream.md. A row is the
          # record that the commit was read and decided — taken or deliberately
          # not — so a release whose commits were taken one by one is not
          # reported as missing. Matched as a table row (never a prose mention)
          # in whichever short form the table writes, 7 or 8 characters.
          missing=0
          while read -r c; do
            [ -n "$c" ] || continue
            s7="$(git rev-parse --short=7 "$c")"
            s8="$(git rev-parse --short=8 "$c")"
            if ! grep -qE "^\| \`(${s7}|${s8})\`" docs/upstream.md; then
              echo "Unrecorded upstream commit: $c"
              missing=1
            fi
          done < <(git rev-list --no-merges "${prev_sha}..${sha}")
          if [ "$missing" = "1" ]; then
            echo "new=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "new=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi
      - name: Say so where a person will see it
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          OWNER: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
          TAG: ${{ steps.newest.outputs.tag }}
          NEW: ${{ steps.newest.outputs.new }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          repo="$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"
          title="Upstream release ${TAG} has not been taken in"
          # Through the REST API rather than the GraphQL one the CLI defaults to:
          # a workflow's own token reads issues either way, but its
          # `createIssue` mutation is refused as "Resource not accessible by
          # integration" however `issues: write` is declared. The REST endpoints
          # are the ones it does carry.
          # Selected by the exact title for this release, so a run for one tag
          # can never comment on or close the issue opened for another.
          open="$(gh api "/repos/${repo}/issues?state=open&per_page=100" \
            | jq -r --arg t "$title" '[.[] | select(.title == $t)][0].number // empty')"
          if [ "$NEW" = "true" ]; then
            {
              echo "@${OWNER} — upstream cut **${TAG}**, and this history has not"
              echo "accounted for it: its commit is not an ancestor of \`main\`, and"
              echo "not every work commit it adds has a row in \`docs/upstream.md\`."
              echo
              echo "- Release: https://git.coffeylabs.org/coffey-labs/ihasmail/releases/tag/${TAG}"
              echo "- Take it in as ADR 0002 says: fetch upstream directly into the"
              echo "  merge, and rename the merged delta before it lands (the"
              echo "  \`gilbert-upstream-rebrand\` checklist). A hand-take that reads"
              echo "  each commit adds its row to \`docs/upstream.md\`, and the next"
              echo "  run closes this."
              echo
              echo "This issue closes itself on the next run once the release is"
              echo "accounted for."
            } > /tmp/upstream-issue.md
            if [ -n "$open" ]; then
              gh api -X POST "/repos/${repo}/issues/${open}/comments" \
                -F body=@/tmp/upstream-issue.md >/dev/null
            else
              # Found by title rather than by label: a label is one more thing
              # to create and keep in step, and this list is never long.
              gh api -X POST "/repos/${repo}/issues" \
                -f title="$title" \
                -F body=@/tmp/upstream-issue.md >/dev/null
            fi
          elif [ -n "$open" ]; then
            # The release is accounted for now — its commit is an ancestor of
            # `main`, or every work commit it adds has a row in
            # `docs/upstream.md` — so whatever this issue was opened for has
            # happened: closing it is the bookkeeping, and it is the only state
            # this watch keeps.
            gh api -X POST "/repos/${repo}/issues/${open}/comments" \
              -f body="The release is accounted for: its commit is an ancestor of \`main\`, or every work commit it adds has a row in \`docs/upstream.md\`." >/dev/null
            gh api -X PATCH "/repos/${repo}/issues/${open}" -f state=closed >/dev/null
          fi
