/**
 * One argument as a JSON Schema, from the tool's own `args` spec.
 *
 * The bound a turn is told and the bound the parser checks come from one place
 * (`ArgSpec`, `tools/define.ts`) — the schema *is* what the turn is told — and a
 * provider that enforces it refuses a wrong type before the step is ever paid
 * for.
 */
function argSchema(spec: ArgSpec): Record<string, unknown> {
  switch (spec.type ?? "text") {
    case "number":
      return {
        type: "integer",
        ...(spec.max === undefined ? {} : { maximum: spec.max }),
      };
    case "boolean":
      return { type: "boolean" };
    case "list":
      return { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } };
    case "one of":
      return {
        type: "string",
        ...(spec.values?.length ? { enum: [...spec.values] } : {}),
      };
    default:
      return {
        type: "string",
        ...(spec.max === undefined ? {} : { maxLength: spec.max }),
      };
  }
}

/** One tool as an OpenAI-compatible completion takes it (ADR 0027). */
export interface ToolDefinition {
  type: "function";
  function: {
    name: string;
    description: string;
    parameters: {
      type: "object";
      properties: Record<string, Record<string, unknown>>;
      additionalProperties: false;
    };
  };
}

/**
 * The catalogue as the provider's own tool definitions, from the same `args`.
 *
 * A model that writes a plan as JSON by hand is guessing at the shape of every
 * argument, and one wrong argument refuses the whole answer (`model_answer_malformed`):
 * a live installation paid refused answers for exactly that — `"id" must be
 * text`, a `fact` over its bound, an argument name the tool does not take. The
 * same definitions are therefore offered as `tools`, so the provider checks the
 * kind and the bound itself (ADR 0027).
 *
 * Nothing is stated twice: the names, the descriptions, the argument names and
 * their bounds are the catalogue's own, and this is the **one** rendering of them
 * the model is given — the system turn carries no second list of the same
 * lines, which were paid for twice on every call.
 * `required` is not set because a key is not the same as a required key (a source
 * is either `from` or `message` with `attachment`), and the tool's parser is the
 * one door that decides.
 */
export function catalogueTools(catalogue: readonly AnyTool[]): ToolDefinition[] {
  return catalogue.map((tool) => ({
    type: "function",
    function: {
      name: tool.name,
      description: tool.description,
      parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: Object.fromEntries(
          tool.keys.map((key) => {
            const spec = tool.args[key];
            /*
             * Every argument a tool takes is declared. One that is not would be
             * guessed at here — `string` for a boolean, `string` for a count —
             * and a guess is what the schema is for not doing: published as a
             * string, `mail.keyword`'s `on` refused the only value it accepts.
             * A tool that names a key and describes no spec is a defect in the
             * tool, so the catalogue refuses to be built rather than hand the
             * model something untrue.
             */
            if (!spec)
              throw new Error(
                `${tool.name} names the argument "${key}" and declares no spec for it.`,
              );
            return [key, argSchema(spec)];
          }),
        ),
        additionalProperties: false,
      },
    },
  }));
}

/**

export const TOOL_LIST_MAX = 200;

/** One optional count, bounded so a model cannot ask the server for a flood. */
export function countArg(
  raw: Record<string, unknown>,
  key: string,
  max: number,
): number | undefined {
  const value = raw[key];
  if (value === undefined || value === null) return undefined;
  if (typeof value !== "number" || !Number.isInteger(value) || value < 1)
    throw new ToolError(
      "bad_arguments",
      `"${key}" must be a whole number of at least 1.`,
    );
  return Math.min(value, max);
}

# ADR 0027 — The agent's tools are described and composable

Status: Accepted

Implementation: Built.
each tool names its arguments, its authority class, the surface it writes and
what it spends, the
arguments are validated before its executor runs, and the half a reading caller
is handed (`readingTools`) is the one that cannot write. The catalogue reaches the
choosing turn **once**: as the provider's own `tools` (`catalogueTools`), each
rendered from the tool's `args` spec, so the schema carries the kind and the bound
the parser checks and a provider that accepts tools refuses a wrong argument
before a step is paid for; the demanded JSON plan is still read, and a call whose
arguments do not fit is refused whole. The installation's one
model is `server/src/agent/model.ts`, and it is chosen at Administration →
Installation (`web/src/views/admin/AdminInstallation.tsx`, whose fields write
the document's `agent.provider`): the key is write-only in the installation's
own document (`shared/installation.ts`, `installationAdmin.ts`) — a save that
states no key, or states an empty one, keeps the stored one, and the `null` a
save states for a provider that needs none clears it — the call is one
...
- The wake is the server's own event stream: a StateChange asks for a pass, and
  the interval is the floor for a mail server that offers none and for the
  pause while a dropped stream is reopened — ten seconds without a working
  stream, thirty with one, because a dated wait kicks a pass directly. A burst
  of changes is one pass, and a change that arrives while a pass runs asks for
  one more.
- The provider's contract is pinned against a stub, and **no real provider has
  answered it**: the first live call is owed before the model path is trusted.
<!-- owed: model-provider-live -->
- The catalogue is offered as **the provider's own tool definitions**, rendered
  from each tool's own `args`: `catalogueTools` is the one rendering, and the
  system turn carries no second list of the same names, descriptions, arguments
  and bounds — the choosing turn is the call every step of every run makes, and
  the same lines twice are paid twice on every call. A call that carries the
  definitions asks the provider to check the kind and the bound of every
  argument, which is what a hand-written JSON plan gets wrong: a live
  installation paid refused answers for a numeric `id`, an over-long `fact` and
  an argument name no tool takes. Every argument a tool names declares its kind,
  and `defineTool` requires it — an argument published as a string because
  nobody said otherwise refuses the value the tool actually takes. `required` is
  not stated, because a key is not a required key and the tool's parser is the
  one door. The demanded JSON shape is still read as the fallback of the same
  call; a gateway that refuses a `tools` field refuses the call loudly, in a
  sentence that names the cause where the provider's own answer names it.

  private async keepClaim(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.claimRenewal) return await this.claimRenewal;
    const expires = this.claimExpires ? Date.parse(this.claimExpires) : 0;
    if (expires - Date.now() > CLAIM_RENEW_WITHIN_MS) return;
    /*
     * Accounts are worked together now, and each write renews the claim when it
     * is close to expiring. One renewal at a time: a second writer waits on the
     * answer of the first rather than sending the same renewal twice.
     */
    this.claimRenewal = (async () => {
      const now = new Date();
      if (!(await renewClaim(this.ctx, this.opts.holder, now)))
        throw new Error("the installation's claim is no longer this process's.");
      this.claimExpires = new Date(now.getTime() + CLAIM_TTL_MS).toISOString();
    })().finally(() => {
      this.claimRenewal = null;
    });
    return await this.claimRenewal;
  }
}

/** The same paths, with this page's reads remembered and the oldest dropped. */
function rememberPaths(
  previous: Record<string, string>,
  found: Map<string, string>,
): Record<string, string> {
  const next: Record<string, string> = { ...previous };
  for (const [id, path] of found) {
    /*
     * Re-set rather than written in place: a node read again moves to the end,
     * so the trim below drops the paths nobody has read for longest. Written in
     * place, a node reported in every page kept the position of its first
     * sighting and could be evicted while an idle one it overtook survived.
     */
    delete next[id];
    next[id] = path;
  }
  const keys = Object.keys(next);
  for (const key of keys.slice(0, Math.max(0, keys.length - MAX_SEEN_NODES)))
    delete next[key];
  return next;
}

const memoryStores = new Map<string, MemoryStore>();

/** One link of the chain per account; the next one runs when this settles. */
function oneAtATime<T>(accountId: string, work: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const previous = memoryWrites.get(accountId) ?? Promise.resolve();

  memoryWrites.set(

    next.then(
      () => undefined,
      () => undefined,
    ),
  );
  return next;
}

export async function destroyAppNode(
  ctx: Ctx,
  accountId: string,
  id: string,
  opts: { ifInState?: string; removeChildren?: boolean } = {},
): Promise<void> {
  const res = await clientOf(ctx).call<SetResponse>(
    FILENODE_SET,
    {
      accountId,
      ...(opts.ifInState ? { ifInState: opts.ifInState } : {}),
      // A folder that still holds something is refused without this, and the
      // folder then goes with everything under it (Stalwart 0.16).
      ...(opts.removeChildren ? { onDestroyRemoveChildren: true } : {}),
      destroy: [id],
    },
    [FILENODE_CAP],
  );
  /*
   * A refusal lands in `notDestroyed` in an otherwise successful response, and
   * reading only the call's own success would report a removal that never
   * happened — a folder still holding something, a lost compare-and-set, a
   * permission. `notFound` is not one of those: the node is already gone, which
   * is the absence the doc above calls success.
   */
  const refused = res.notDestroyed?.[id];
  if (refused && refused.type !== "notFound")
    throw new AppFolderError(refusalOf(refused));
}

/**
 * Move or rename a node.
 *
 * Beside the destroy because it is the other way a level's membership changes.
 * A `parentId` of `null` is the top level of Files, which is a place rather than

# ADR 0037 — The reading cursor is a document

Status: Proposed

Implementation: Built. `server/src/agent/cursors.ts` — `readCursor`,
`writeCursor` and the `gilbert/cursors.json` document in each group's own app
folder — and `server/src/agent/loop.ts`, which restores it on a process's first
pass (`restoreCursor`), writes it after a batch that moved the reading
(`saveCursor`), and says an unreadable one in the pass's gaps. The write hands
back the state it produced and the cursor takes it, so a quiet account writes
nothing; `events.ts` counts the document as the agent's own, so writing it wakes
no rule.

## Context

A pass reads each account's change log from where the last one ended, and the
cursor it keeps is the state the server answered for that read (ADR 0030, ADR
0032). A cursor that exists only in the loop's memory is a cursor that begins
each process by anchoring at the state the server holds **then**, which is not a
resumption but a fresh start: every change that arrived while the process was

**The cursor is a document, per account, in that account's own app folder** —
`gilbert/cursors.json`, beside the runs, the rules and the drop queue — carrying
the three states the reading ended at (`mail`, `files`, `calendar`), the paths it
learned for destroyed nodes (`seen`), and the instant of the read that produced it.

- **It is read on a process's first pass for that account** and taken as the
  cursor; a process that finds none anchors where the server stands, which is the
  first read of a group and the only time a window can be lost unseen.
- **It is written after a batch the pass answered**, and only when the reading
  moved: a quiet account writes nothing, so a cursor never becomes a heartbeat.
- **An unreadable document is a gap the pass says out loud**, and the reading
  anchors afresh — the same ending `cannotCalculateChanges` has. A cursor guessed
  at from a shape this build cannot read would be a window reported as ordinary.
- **`at` is part of the document** because the off path's freshness question
  ("a cursor nobody advanced for an hour") is the cursor's age, and that age has
  to survive a restart for the answer to be the same one.

## Consequences

- A restart resumes instead of forgetting: a deployment no longer eats the mail,
  the chat messages and the file drops that arrived while the service was down,
  and a dropped window becomes a claim the installation can check rather than a
  silence.
- One more write per account per batch that moved, in Stalwart, where the runs
  already are; the cursor is small and is not rewritten when nothing moved.
- A cursor document is now something an operator can read to answer "what has the
  agent seen?", which is the question the live failure could not answer.
=== FEATURES 112-122 ===

The agent works one group at a time, from the mail server's change log, inside
that group's own account and as the installation's Master. It does the
reversible work itself, and it stops wherever a person is answerable. **What it
has read is a document** — `gilbert/cursors.json` in each group's app folder
(ADR 0037) — so a restart, a deploy or a crash resumes where the last process
stopped instead of anchoring at the present and losing what arrived in between.

**It does:** reads inside documents and attachments; files and labels mail;
keeps the label catalog and the folders; drafts a reply to everyone; settles a
workorder step; proposes a KB page; writes and moves documents; creates events in
the group's own calendar; says what it did; asks a person; remembers facts.

/**
 * The instant the run's wait comes due, or null when it has none.
 *
 * The run's own answer to "is it waiting, and until when", and the one place it
 * is given: a run that is running or **blocked on a person with a deadline** is
 * waiting, and a dated wait beside any other ending is not — a date on a stopped
 * run is not a wait, and firing it would start a run whose end nobody re-opened.
 * Both readers of the answer ask it here — the process that arms the waits
 * (`agent/timers.ts`) and the question of whether one has come due (`isRunDue`) —
 * so the two cannot drift apart on a dateless or an ended run.
 */
export function waitDueAt(run: RunDoc): string | null {
  if (run.state !== "running" && run.state !== "blocked") return null;
  return run.waiting?.until ?? null;
}

/** Whether the run's wait has come due at `now`. */
export function isRunDue(run: RunDoc, now: Date): boolean {
  const until = waitDueAt(run);
  return until !== null && Date.parse(until) <= now.getTime();
}

=== archive ===
 * The month a run's drawer is named after, from the instant it ended — or null
 * for a run still running, which is never archived.
 */
export function archiveMonth(run: RunRecord["run"]): string | null {
  // A run still working, or one parked on a person, is not closed: the answer
  // that comes back is recognised against the working set, and a drawer has no
  // reader for it.
  if (run.state === "running" || run.state === "blocked") return null;
  const at = run.ended?.at;
  if (typeof at !== "string") return null;
  const ended = new Date(at);
  if (!Number.isFinite(ended.getTime())) return null;
  // The server's own clock, as its log lines read: a run ended late on the last
  // day of a month stays in that month.
  return `${ended.getFullYear()}-${String(ended.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, "0")}`;
}

 * The administration surface of the installation's agent, end to end against the

 *
 * The three documents live in three accounts and the door reaches all of them as
 * the installation, so the suite signs in as the demo administrator (the one
 * holding the admin marker) and writes its fixtures the way the agent does: as the
 * Master, with its own credential, in the Master's `memory/` folder and in the
 * group's `runs/` folder. That is what makes the read assertions honest — the
 * routes reach those accounts by impersonation, not by handing themselves a

 *
 * Three mechanisms are pinned, each with the mutation that reddens it:
 *
 * - **the runs are drawn as the record carries them**, and a document of a

 *   rather than dropped or drawn blank (remove the `problem` branch and the
 *   unreadable run disappears; draw it as an empty run and the listing lies);
 * - **a fact an administrator corrects is saved through the admin door** — in the
 *   Master's own account, with the correcting person stamped on it, and the
 *   agent's own write refused against it afterwards (answer the route `ok`
 *   without writing and the store still holds the old sentence);
 * - **a lapsed claim is no claim**, because the instant ADR 0032 gives it means
 *   one thing.
 */

const DEMO_AUTH = `Basic ${Buffer.from(`${DEMO}:demo-password`).toString("base64")}`;

/** The group account the runs are written into, as the demo session holds it. */

before(async () => {
  // The installation's agent: impersonated from the administrator's session, so
  // the routes reach the Master's account without a deployment credential.
  config.agent.address = MASTER;
  config.agent.password = "";

    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify({ username: DEMO, password: "demo-password" }),

    username: MASTER,

  );
  assert.ok(team, "the demo session is a member of the group whose runs are read");
  teamAccount = team[0];
});

        plan: ["read the mail"],
      }),
      "file it, if the mail was read",
      { step: 0, when: "done" },
    ),
    0,
    { state: "done", outcome: "read one message" },

      rule: string | null;
      woke: string | null;
      steps: number;
      spent: { calls: number };
      problem: string | null;
    }>;
  };
  const listed = runs.find((row) => row.id === "surface-run");
  assert.ok(listed, "the run the group worked is in the listing");
  assert.equal(listed.state, "running", "the list says how it stands");
  assert.equal(listed.woke, "mail created: m-1", "with the change that woke it");
  assert.equal(listed.rule, "intake", "and the rule that answered it");
  assert.equal(listed.steps, 2, "and how many steps it carries");
  assert.equal(listed.spent.calls, 0, "and the tally of what it spent");
  assert.equal(listed.problem, null, "a run this build reads has no problem");

  assert.equal(shown.plan[0]?.outcome, "read one message", "with what the step answered");

  assert.match(

    "the reason names the path",
  );
  assert.ok(
    rows.some((row) => row.id === "surface-run"),
    "and the runs this build reads are still on the surface beside it",
  );
});

export function isPassStatusDoc(x: unknown): x is PassStatusDoc {
  const ended = isRecord(x) ? (x as { lastEnded?: unknown }).lastEnded : undefined;
  return (
    isRecord(x) &&
    (x.v === undefined || typeof x.v === "number") &&
    isInstant(x.at) &&
    isFiniteNumber(x.ms) &&
    typeof x.claimed === "boolean" &&
    isCount(x.accounts) &&
    isCount(x.changes) &&
    isCount(x.runs) &&
    isCount(x.due) &&
    Array.isArray(x.gaps) &&
    x.gaps.every((one) => typeof one === "string") &&
    (ended === undefined ||
      (isRecord(ended) &&
        typeof ended.id === "string" &&
        !!ended.id &&
        isRunEnding(ended.ending) &&
        typeof ended.why === "string"))
  );
}

/** A finite number, whole or not: a duration in milliseconds. */
function isFiniteNumber(x: unknown): x is number {
  return typeof x === "number" && Number.isFinite(x);
}

/** A whole, finite count: what every tally on the pass's own document is. */
function isCount(x: unknown): x is number {
  return typeof x === "number" && Number.isInteger(x) && x >= 0;
}

/**
 * How many elements a folder holds, one level down: the files and the folders
 * directly inside it, nothing further.
 *
 * The server counts the level, so this asks for one id and reads the total
 * rather than downloading the folder to count what came back. A server that
 * answers no total leaves the page it sent as the count.
 */
export async function countChildren(accountId: Id, parentId: Id | null): Promise<number> {
  const { list, total } = await listChildrenWithState(accountId, parentId, ["id"], {
    limit: 1,
    total: true,
  });
  return total ?? list.length;
}

/**
 * A record in the tray, the one place a failure is reported.

 * both the same value, and the second one's progress would then move the first
=== fileSort ===
 * a Size sort that scattered folders through the files would be sorting by
 * nothing. Within each of the two groups the column decides, and a tie on the
 * column falls back to the name, so the order is the same on two devices.
 */
export function sortFiles(
  nodes: FileNode[],
  sort: FilesSort,
  /**
   * What a folder holds, when the caller has counted it: the Size column shows
   * that number for a folder, so it is what the column sorts by — a column whose
   * value and sort key disagree orders by something the reader cannot see.
   */
  folderCounts?: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
): FileNode[] {
  const rank = (n: FileNode) => (n.nodeType === "directory" ? 0 : 1);
  const byName = (a: FileNode, b: FileNode) =>
    a.name.localeCompare(b.name, undefined, { sensitivity: "base", numeric: true });
  /* `UTCDate` is an ISO-8601 instant in UTC (`jmap/types.ts`), so the strings
     compare in time order and no parsing is needed to order two of them. */
  const stamp = (n: FileNode) => n.modified ?? n.created;
  const size = (n: FileNode) =>
    n.nodeType === "directory" ? (folderCounts?.[n.id] ?? 0) : (n.size ?? 0);
  return [...nodes].sort((a, b) => {
    if (rank(a) !== rank(b)) return rank(a) - rank(b);
    let by: number;
    if (sort.key === "name") by = byName(a, b);
    else if (sort.key === "size") by = size(a) - size(b);
    else by = stamp(a).localeCompare(stamp(b));
    if (by === 0) return byName(a, b);
    return sort.desc ? -by : by;
  });

   * The account being browsed, which is not always the reader's own.
   *
   * Files is the one module that opens somebody else's account in place: a
   * folder shared with you is reached from "Shared with me" in the tree, not by
   * switching the whole app over. So this moves and `ownAccountId` does not,
   * and anything belonging to the reader -- their settings, their signatures --
   * goes through `ownAccountFor` rather than either of them.

  accountId: Id | null;

  ownAccountId: Id | null;

  sharedAccounts: SharedAccount[];

  listingShown: { parentId: Id | null } | null;

     * row on screen is not always the one the run began with (a folder of two

    runId: string;

function mergeTree(accountId: Id, root: FileNode, signal: AbortSignal): MergeTree {
  const levels = new Map<Id, FileNode[]>();
  return {
    root,
    async childrenOf(parentId) {
      signal.throwIfAborted();
      const held = levels.get(parentId);
      if (held) return held;
      const list = await readChildren(accountId, parentId, signal);
      levels.set(parentId, list);
      return list;
    },
  };
}

 * directly inside it, nothing further.
 *

 * rather than downloading the folder to count what came back. **A server that

export async function countChildren(

    limit: 1,
    total: true,
  });

    /**
     * Create an address book, owned by `accountId` when given and by the
     * reader's own account otherwise. A book created on a group account
     * belongs to the group: it is written directly into the group's own
     * account, so every member -- including one added after the fact --
     * reaches it through their session on that account, and no share or
     * per-user ACL is written. Group books are created subscribed so members
     * see them without each adding one; the reader's own books need no flag
     * (they are theirs, listed as such).
     */
    async createBook(name, accountId?: Id) {
      const own = get().accountId!;
      const target = accountId ?? own;
      const res = await client.call<SetResponse<AddressBook>>("AddressBook/set", {
        accountId: target,
        create: { b: target === own ? { name } : { name, isSubscribed: true } },
      });
      const err = res.notCreated?.b;
      if (err) throw new Error(setErrorMessage(err));
      if (target === own) await get().loadBooks();
      else await get().reloadShared();
      return res.created!.b!.id;

Let me be concrete with the code:

- `decideEvent` had return type `Promise<ModelAnswer>` where `ModelAnswer = decision | read | reply`.
- But at runtime, `read` never escapes: the loop inside `decideEvent` performs the read, pushes the result into `reads`, and asks the model again. It either returns `decision`/`reply` or throws (max reads exhausted / malformed).
- The caller (changes.ts) did: `if (decision.kind === "reply") { ...; continue; }` then `if (decision.kind !== "decision") { ... notice ...; continue; }` then used `decision.rules`, `decision.facts`.
- That second `if` was the only thing making TypeScript narrow to `decision` — because the static type still included `read`. The body was unreachable in behaviour (a `read` can never come back), so the reviewer called it dead code, correctly.
- I removed it → typecheck: `Property 'rules' does not exist on type ... | {kind:"read"...}`.
- Two ways to fix: (a) put the branch back (a guard nobody can ever hit, kept only to satisfy the compiler — a workaround, and it lies about the protocol: it would silently swallow a `read` if it ever did escape); (b) make the type say the truth: the function never answers with a `read`, so its return type is `decision | reply` (`DecisionAnswer = Exclude<ModelAnswer, {kind:"read"}>`). - Why it's the root fix: the type was wider than the behaviour. The mismatch is the cause; the dead branch was a symptom of it. Also worth noting: the branch, if it had ever fired, would have skipped the change entirely (continue) — i.e. a read escaping would have meant "the change is silently dropped". So the branch wasn't just dead; it was a trap.

## Cosa è successo

`decideEvent` dichiarava `Promise<ModelAnswer>`, e `ModelAnswer` ha tre varianti:

```ts
{ kind: "decision"; rules; facts } | { kind: "read"; name; args } | { kind: "reply"; text }
```

Ma `read` **non esce mai** da quella funzione: il turno di decisione la esegue lui (`runTool(READING_TOOLS, …)`), mette il risultato in `reads`, e richiama il modello. La funzione quindi fa `return` solo per `decision` e `reply`, oppure lancia (letture esaurite, risposta malformata). Il tipo, però, era più largo del comportamento.

## Perché il ramo sembrava morto — e lo era

In `changes.ts` il codice era:

```ts
if (decision.kind === "reply") { …; continue; }
if (decision.kind !== "decision") { …avviso…; continue; }   // ← questo
const chosen = mentioned ? mentionRoute(decision.rules, …) : decision.rules;
```

Dopo il primo `if`, TypeScript restringe a `decision | read` — perché il tipo dice ancora che `read` è possibile. Il secondo `if` era **l'unica cosa** che restringeva a `decision`, e il suo corpo non poteva mai essere raggiunto. La review l'ha chiamato ramo morto, correttamente.

Ma non era solo inutile: se un `read` fosse mai arrivato, quel ramo avrebbe fatto `continue` — cioè avrebbe **scartato il cambiamento in silenzio**. Un guardiano per un caso impossibile che, se il caso diventasse possibile, sbaglia.

## Perché toglierlo ha rotto la compilazione

`tsc` ha detto:

```
changes.ts(581,54): Property 'rules' does not exist on type
  { kind: "decision"; … } | { kind: "read"; … }
```

Il narrowing non c'era più, e il tipo diceva la verità: `read` potrebbe arrivare. Il difetto non era nel ramo rimosso, era **nel tipo troppo largo**. Il ramo era il sintomo.

## Le due strade, e perché ho scelto la seconda

1. **Rimetti il ramo.** Il codice torna a compilare, ma resta una guardia per un caso che non esiste, tenuta solo per far contento il compilatore: un workaround. E continua a mentire sul protocollo — dice "potrebbe arrivare una lettura", mentre la funzione la consuma sempre.
2. **Stringi il tipo a ciò che la funzione fa davvero.** Una riga sola:

```ts
export type DecisionAnswer = Exclude<ModelAnswer, { kind: "read" }>;
// decideEvent(…): Promise<DecisionAnswer>
```

Così il narrowing avviene **alla fonte**: chi chiama riceve due varianti, non tre, e non porta un ramo per un caso che non può accadere. E se domani qualcuno cambia `decideEvent` in modo che un `read` sfugga davvero, il compilatore lo obbliga a dirlo nel tipo, invece di lasciare che venga trattato come "nessuna decisione" e il cambiamento sparisca.

## Perché è la stessa famiglia di difetto

È lo stesso schema di `v: 1` nel documento di stato: **il tipo afferma più (o meno) di ciò che il codice fa**. Lì il tipo diceva `v: 1` mentre il validatore accettava qualsiasi numero; qui il tipo diceva "può rispondere con una lettura" mentre la funzione non lo fa. In entrambi i casi la correzione non è aggiungere un controllo, è far dire al tipo la verità — così i controlli non servono più.

Il ramo rimosso non era una svista mia: era un ramo che esisteva per un tipo sbagliato.

import { DEFAULT_SETTINGS, useSettings } from "@/store/settings";
import { fakeJmapServer } from "@/test/jmapServer";

/*
 * Saving the people you write to as contacts. What has to hold: only addresses
 * no card holds yet are added, never the sender's own; the book is created once
 * and remembered by id, adopted where one already has its name, and replaced
 * when it has been deleted; and a message sent from a group's mailbox collects
 * nothing -- the group's correspondents are not the reader's.
 */

const SESSION = {
  accounts: {
    r: { name: "me@example.org", isPersonal: true },
    g: { name: "team@example.org", isPersonal: false },
  },
  primaryAccounts: { [CAP.contacts]: "r" },
  capabilities: {},
  state: "s1",
} as unknown as JmapSession;

function server() {
  return fakeJmapServer()
    .on("AddressBook/set", () => ({
      accountId: "r",
      oldState: "1",
      newState: "2",
      created: { b: { id: "bk-collected" } },
      notCreated: null,
    }))
    .on("AddressBook/get", () => ({
      accountId: "r",
      state: "1",
      list: [{ id: "bk-collected", name: "Collected" }],
      notFound: [],
    }))
    .on("ContactCard/set", (call) => {
      const create = (call.args.create ?? {}) as Record<string, unknown>;
      return {
        accountId: "r",
        oldState: "1",
        newState: "2",
        created: Object.fromEntries(
          Object.keys(create).map((k) => [k, { id: `k-${k}` }]),
        ),
        notCreated: null,
      };
    });
}

export async function forgetFact(ctx: Ctx, accountId: string, id: string): Promise<void> {
  return await oneAtATime(
    accountId,
    () => listFacts(ctx, accountId),
    async (opening) => {

          ifInState: opening.state,
          onState,
        }),

      if (state) memoryStores.set(accountId, { ...opening, state });

  );

   * has moved since is refused rather than landing over what somebody else

   * only case the token decides: a test whose store never moves writes the same
   * bytes with or without it.

    accountId,
    {
      subject: "Oltremare",
      fact: "the usual shipper for the northern route",
      run: "r-1",
      at: AT,
      group: accountId,
    },
    await store(),
  );

      run: "r-1",
      at: AT,
      group: accountId,
    },

          who: "admin@example.com",
          at: AT,
        },

      ),

    "the correction loses the compare-and-set and is refused, not applied",

    "the usual shipper for the northern route",
    "and the sheet the stale correction meant to change is left as it was",
  );

  await assert.rejects(
    () => forgetFact(ctx, accountId, first.id, stale),
    refused,
    "and the removal, decided against the same stale reading, is refused too",
  );
  assert.ok(
    await readFact(ctx, accountId, first.id),
    "so the fact is still in the memory",
  );

test("a mention no rule covers is answered rather than left in silence", async () => {
  /*
   * A group whose rules say nothing about the conversation has no agent there —
   * but the person still addressed it, and silence is not an answer to a question
   * somebody typed.
   */
  const agent = loop();
  await agent.start();
  await postChatMessage(ctx, accountId, "sam@example.org", "@gilbert anybody there?");
  await agent.pass();

  const said = await findChatMessages(ctx, accountId, "no rule for the conversation", 5);
  assert.equal(said.length, 1, "the person is told why nothing happened");
  assert.ok(said[0]?.replyTo, "in the thread they wrote in");
});

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# OpenCode mesh client: point this machine's OpenCode client at another
# machine's OpenCode server over the Tailscale mesh.
#
# Invocation:
#   opencode-<peer> [opencode args...]     via the symlink of the same name
#   opencode-peer <peer> [opencode args...]
#
# A peer's URL and password come from ~/.config/opencode/<peer>.env, which
# defines OPENCODE_<PEER>_SERVER and OPENCODE_PASSWORD. The peer is the file
# basename; a `-` in the peer name becomes `_` in the variable name.
#
#   opencode-ai                    # full TUI against ai
#   opencode-ai ~/git/project      # TUI against ai, opened in a directory
#   opencode-ai api get /api/info  # API request against ai
#
# The opencode client binary is resolved robustly (OPENCODE_BIN > PATH >
# nvm bin > ~/.opencode/bin > /usr/local/bin) because a non-login process
# does not have nvm's bin on PATH.
#
# `--server` is a per-subcommand flag in this client build: it is accepted
# after a subcommand that declares it, never before the subcommand. Only the
# subcommands listed below can target a remote server; the plain TUI form
# targets it through the top-level flag.
set -euo pipefail

self="$(basename -- "$0")"
if [ "$self" = opencode-peer ]; then
  peer="${1:?usage: opencode-peer <peer> [opencode args...]}"
  shift
else
  peer="${self#opencode-}"
fi

env_file="${OPENCODE_PEER_ENV:-$HOME/.config/opencode/${peer}.env}"
if [ ! -r "$env_file" ]; then
  echo "opencode-peer: cannot read $env_file" >&2
  exit 1
fi

<skill_content name="gilbert-ui">
# Skill: gilbert-ui

# Gilbert — one visual language

The client is one product with one shell: a control means the same thing on
every surface, and a surface that needs something new extends the shared
primitive rather than inventing a second one. This skill is the working half of
the single-source rule: code↔code duplication is a defect, and **a second visual
spelling of the same action is that defect wearing a costume**.

## Before you add a control

1. **Name the action.** "Save to Files", "Create", "Select all". Then find how
   the app already says it: `grep -rn` for the class and for the label
   (`grep -rn 'Save to Files' web/src`). If a surface already does it, reuse —
   including the icon.
2. **Find the primitive, not the nearest copy.** `web/src/ui/` holds the shared
   ones: `dialog.tsx` (Dialog, confirmDialog, promptDialog), `popover.tsx`
   (Popover, MenuItem, MenuSep, MenuTitle), `toast.tsx`, `tabs.tsx`,
   `SectionShell.tsx`, `misc.tsx` (`Empty`), `LoadState.tsx`, `selection.tsx`,
   `datefield.tsx`, `JsonDocumentEditor.tsx`, `Splitter.tsx`.
3. **If the pattern is wrong, fix the pattern.** A local override that makes one
   surface look right leaves the next surface wrong. Correct the class, the
   shared component or the token, and every caller inherits it.

## The classes and what they mean

- **Buttons** (`.btn` in `styles/app.css`): one primary action per surface
  (`.btn-primary`), secondary as `.btn` with a border or `.btn-ghost` without —
  **not both for the same weight**, destructive as `.btn-danger` and set apart
  from the group. Sizes `.btn-sm` / `.btn-lg`; icon-only is `.icon-btn`
  (`.sm`, `.xs`). An icon-only control carries a `title` and an `aria-label`.
- **Icons**: lucide only, one meaning per glyph across the app (a folder for
  "put it in Files", an arrow-into-tray for "put it on this machine"; never an
  arrow pointing up for a save). Sizes 14 (inside a button or a row), 16–18
  (toolbar), 22 (list header illustration). Same family and direction for a pair
  of sibling actions.
- **Empty states**: `Empty` (`ui/misc.tsx`) — icon, title, one line. Every
  surface uses it; nobody writes a bespoke "nothing here" paragraph.
- **Loading**: a `.spinner` for a pane that has nothing yet; a carried window
  plus the two-pixel `.list-loading` bar when the previous content can stay. Never
  draw placeholder rows for content that is about to arrive.
- **Counters and badges**: one markup per idea — `.nav-count` for a folder's
  unread count, a `.tag` for a label, a badge only for a pending queue. A number
  in a new pill is a new visual language.
- **Tags and chips**: `.tag` (a label), `.folder-tag` (where a row lives),
  `.attachment` (a file, whole chip clickable, `.viewable` cursor `zoom-in`).
- **Colours and spacing come from tokens**: `var(--bg)`, `--bg-elev`,
  `--bg-sunken`, `--read-bg`, `--border`, `--fg*`, `--accent*`, `--danger`,
  `--radius*`, `--shadow*`. No hex in a component, no new elevation. Spacing is
  the 4/8 scale already in use (`4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 24`), not arbitrary pixels.
- **Truncation**: `text-overflow: ellipsis` with the full value in `title`; a
  chip that clips mid-word without a title is a defect.
- **Tables**: header in the same case everywhere (small caps is the app's), the
  numeric column right-aligned, a row menu in the last cell.
- **Destructive actions**: separated from the neutral group (spacing or a
  divider) and never styled exactly like "Save". Deleting a draft, emptying a
  folder, removing an account are not one grey icon among five.

## Surfaces that must agree

Mail, Calendar, Contacts, Files, KB, Chat, Workorders, Settings, Administration.
For each, the same question asked the same way: does the toolbar carry the
primary action once? do the section headings read the same? do the actions of a
row sit in the same place? An action added in one surface is checked against the
others before it ships.

## The shell tells no lies

The top bar is the same on every surface, so anything in it must be true
everywhere: a search box that queries mail is labelled and behaves as mail (or
is contextual), not presented as the global search of the product. A section
title with no items under it is removed, not left as decoration.

## Process

- **Design the exception out.** A one-off that "looks better here" is either
  promoted to the shared primitive or dropped.
- **A visual pass is read-only first**: walk the surfaces at a real viewport,
  collect the divergences with their route and element, rank them, and let the
  owner choose — the same discipline as a code review, ending in decisions.
- **The inventory above is the current state**: when a primitive changes, this
  file changes in the same diff (snapshot mode, no history).
- **i18n**: every new label is a `t()`/`tc()`/`plural()` key — see
  `gilbert-i18n`; a control is not done until its words are.

  emptyMetrics,
  type MetricsPeriod,
  periodSince,
  type RunMetrics,
} from "./metrics";

   * One reader for the page, two rhythms: the whole history every sixty

   * The running answer is a few rows, so a poll every three seconds does not
   * carry a year of documents.
   */
  useEffect(() => {

    const stopPush = push.subscribe((changed, type) => {

       * act on, and stopping it is that act.

          {inFlight.map((entry) => (

                          : row,
                      ),
                    )
                  }
                />
              </div>
              <div style={{ display: "grid", gap: 6 }}>
                {entry.rows.map(({ listed }) => (
                  <div key={listed.id} className="run-current">
                    <span className={`run-state run-state-${listed.state}`}>
                      {listed.state && t(RUN_STATE_LABELS[listed.state])}
                    </span>
                    <span className="run-row-id">{listed.id}</span>
                    {listed.rule && <span className="run-row-meta">{listed.rule}</span>}
                    {listed.woke && <span className="run-row-meta">{listed.woke}</span>}
                    <StopRun
                      group={entry.group}
                      id={listed.id}
                      onStopped={() =>
                        setLive((held) =>
                          held.map((row) =>
                            row.group === entry.group
                              ? {
                                  ...row,
                                  runs: row.runs.filter((one) => one.id !== listed.id),
                                }
                              : row,
                          ),
                        )
                      }
                    />
                  </div>
                ))}
              </div>
            </div>
          ))}
        </section>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

    const poll = () => {

    const fallback = window.setInterval(poll, 10_000);
    let scheduled: number | null = null;
    const stopPush = accountId

          if (!alive || type !== "FileNode" || changed !== accountId) return;
          if (scheduled !== null) return;
          scheduled = window.setTimeout(() => {
            scheduled = null;
            poll();
          }, 1_000);
        })
      : () => {};
    return () => {
      alive = false;

      stopPush();

   * left on an empty page, and the clamp is an effect so the render that first

  useEffect(() => {

function isStart(x: unknown): x is RunStart {
  if (!isRecord(x)) return false;
  const { rule, instruction, woke } = x;
  // A field this build writes is a field it requires: a document missing one is
  // a document this build did not write.
  if (!("woke" in x)) return false;
  if (rule !== null && (typeof rule !== "string" || !rule)) return false;
  if (instruction !== null && !isMessageRef(instruction)) return false;
  if (woke !== null && (typeof woke !== "string" || !woke.trim())) return false;
  if ("sends" in x && typeof x.sends !== "boolean") return false;
  if ("batch" in x) {
    const batch = (x as { batch?: unknown }).batch;
    if (
      !Array.isArray(batch) ||
      !batch.every((one) => typeof one === "string" && one !== "")
    )
      return false;
  }
  const wakeFrom = (x as { wakeFrom?: unknown }).wakeFrom;

 */
async function aboutOf(
  ctx: Ctx,
  event: AccountEvent,
  message: ChatMessage | null,
  mail: { subject?: string | null; text?: string } | null,
): Promise<string | undefined> {
  if (message?.text) return clipAbout(message.text);

    const subject = mail?.subject ?? mail?.text;
    if (subject) return clipAbout(subject);
  }
  if (event.source === "files") {

  }
  return undefined;
}

/** One line, bounded: the surfaces draw it in a row, and the document is not a log. */
function clipAbout(text: string): string | undefined {
  const line = text.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
  if (!line) return undefined;
  return line.length > ABOUT_MAX ? `${line.slice(0, ABOUT_MAX - 1)}…` : line;
}

function messageTextOf(message: Record<string, unknown>): string {
  const values = isRecord(message.bodyValues) ? message.bodyValues : {};

```ts
async function aboutOf(
  ctx: Ctx,
  accountId: string,
  event: AccountEvent,
  message: { text?: string; from?: string | null } | null,
  mail: { subject?: string | null; from?: string | null } | null,
): Promise<{ about?: string; by?: string }> {
  if (message?.text) return { about: clipAbout(message.text), ...(message.from ? { by: message.from } : {}) };
  if (event.source === "mail" && mail) {
    const line = mail.subject ?? undefined;
    return { ...(line ? { about: clipAbout(line) } : {}), ...(mail.from ? { by: mail.from } : {}) };
  }
  if (event.source === "files") {
    const names = [event.where, ...(event.also ?? [])];
    const line = clipAbout(names.join(", "));
    return line ? { about: line } : {};
  }
  if (event.source === "calendar" && event.change !== "destroyed") {
    const found = await clientOf(ctx).call<{list?: Array<Record<string, unknown>>}>("CalendarEvent/get", {accountId, ids: [event.where]}, [CAPABILITIES.calendars]).catch(() => null);
    const title = found?.list?.[0]?.title;
    if (typeof title === "string") { const line = clipAbout(title); if (line) return { about: line }; }
  }
  return {};
}
```

    <section>
      <h2>{t("Runs")}</h2>
      {metrics && (
        <p className="hint">
          {t(
            "{runs} runs · {calls} model calls · {failed} failed steps · {tokens} tokens",
            {
              runs: metrics.runs,
              calls: metrics.calls,
              failed: metrics.failed,
              tokens: metrics.promptTokens + metrics.completionTokens,
            },
          )}
        </p>
      )}
      <label className="run-archive">
        <span className="hint">{t("Archived")}</span>
        <input
          type="month"
          value={month}
          aria-label={t("Archived")}
          onChange={(event) => setMonth(event.target.value)}
        />
        {month && (
          <button type="button" className="btn btn-ghost" onClick={() => setMonth("")}>
            {t("Current runs")}
          </button>
        )}
      </label>
      {error && <div className="error-box">{error}</div>}
      {!error && !runs && <p className="hint">{t("Loading…")}</p>}
      {runs && runs.length === 0 && <p className="hint">{t("Nothing here yet.")}</p>}
      <div style={{ marginTop: 12 }}>
        {shown.map((row) => (
          <RunRow
            key={row.id}
            group={group}
            row={row}
            month={month}
            facts={facts}
            onStopped={() => void load()}
          />
        ))}
      </div>
      {pages > 1 && (
        <div style={{ display: "flex", gap: 8, alignItems: "center", marginTop: 12 }}>
          <button
            type="button"
            className="btn btn-ghost"
            disabled={page === 0}
            onClick={() => setPage((p) => Math.max(0, p - 1))}
          >
            {t("Previous")}
          </button>
          <span className="hint">
            {page + 1} / {pages}
          </span>
          <button
            type="button"
            className="btn btn-ghost"
            disabled={(page >= pages - 1 && !more) || loadingMore}
            onClick={() => {
              if (page >= pages - 1 && more) {
                void loadMore().then((loaded) => {
                  if (loaded) setPage((p) => p + 1);
                });
                return;
              }
              setPage((p) => Math.min(pages - 1, p + 1));
            }}
          >
            {t("Next")}
          </button>
        </div>
      )}
    </section>
  );

/**

 * the plan with the step it is on.
 */
function LiveRun({ group, row, onStopped }: { group: string; row: RunSummary; onStopped: () => void }) {
  return (
    <div className="run-current" style={{ marginBottom: 6 }}>
      <div className="row" style={{ gap: 8, alignItems: "center", flexWrap: "wrap" }}>
        <span className={`run-state run-state-${row.state}`}>{row.state && t(RUN_STATE_LABELS[row.state])}</span>
        <span className="run-row-id">{row.id}</span>
        {row.rule && <span className="run-row-meta">{row.rule}</span>}
        {row.openedAt && <span className="run-row-meta">{formatFullDate(row.openedAt)}</span>}
        <StopRun group={group} id={row.id} onStopped={onStopped} />
      </div>
      {(row.about ?? row.woke) && (
        <p className="hint" style={{ margin: "4px 0 0" }} title={(row.about ?? row.woke) ?? undefined}>
          {row.by
            ? t("{what} — from {who}", { what: row.about ?? row.woke ?? "", who: row.by })
            : (row.about ?? row.woke)}
        </p>
      )}
      <RunPlan steps={row.plan ?? []} />
    </div>
  );
}

/**

 * the bound it is held to.
 *
 * The **one** rendering both turns use (`catalogueLines`). The schema a provider
 * receives is a hint it may ignore — a live model sent `maxLength` and answered
 * with a `fact` five times over it — while the same bound in words is what it
 * follows. So the line carries the kind and the bound as prose, and the tools
 * carry the schema: the two read the same `ArgSpec`.
 */
export function toolLine(tool: AnyTool): string {
  const args = tool.keys.length
    ? tool.keys.map((key) => argText(key, tool.args[key]!)).join(", ")
    : "no arguments";
  return `- ${tool.name}(${args}): ${tool.description}`;
}

/** One argument as a phrase: its name, its kind, and the bound it is held to. */
function argText(key: string, spec: ArgSpec): string {
  const bound =
    spec.min !== undefined && spec.max !== undefined
      ? ` ${spec.min}–${spec.max}`
      : spec.min !== undefined
        ? ` ≥${spec.min}`
        : spec.max !== undefined
          ? ` ≤${spec.max}`
          : "";

      ? `one of ${(spec.values ?? []).join("|")}`
      : spec.type === "list"
        ? `list of text${bound}`
        : `${spec.type}${bound}`;
  return `${key}: ${kind}${spec.about ? ` — ${spec.about}` : ""}`;
}

/** The catalogue as prose, one tool per line: what both turns show. */
export function catalogueLines(tools: readonly AnyTool[]): string[] {
  return tools.map(toolLine);
}

function nearestTool(

  name: string,
  problem: string,
): string {

  return `${problem} The ${surface} tools are: ${same.join(", ")}.`;

1. **La `rules.json` legacy (A9).** È un documento vecchio, in forma pre-ADR-0031, che sembra la regola viva e non lo è. Le strade sono due e cambiano il prodotto: **migrarlo** (leggerlo una volta e riscrivere le sue regole in `rules/`, poi archiviarlo — ma la forma vecchia ha `trigger`/`capabilities`, quindi va deciso *come* tradurla) oppure **archiviarlo e dirlo nel pass** (nessun rischio, il file sparisce dalla vista). Non lo faccio da solo perché la prima è una decisione di prodotto.
2. **`wakeFrom` sbagliato (A7).** Serve **un** dato: il documento di chat di quel messaggio e l'indirizzo della sessione di chi l'ha scritto. Con quello si vede se il torto è nel documento o nella lettura, e si corregge alla radice invece di indovinare.
3. **`ifInState` (B6).** La metà memoria è già risolta (confronto per foglio). Restano le scritture dell'account: per attribuirle serve **quale** scrittura rifiuta, e il messaggio oggi non lo dice. È una riga di log da aggiungere, non un'indagine.

## Quello che invece è già deciso da me e non richiede te

- **B9**: il modello non sa quanti passi gli restano. La riga nel prompt con il budget residuo è piccola e va fatta — è l'unico modo perché un piano troppo grande sia colpa sua, non del loop.
- **I test d'invariante** dei meccanismi nuovi: vanno scritti prima di dire "fatto", altrimenti la prossima indagine ritrova gli stessi buchi.

## La domanda vera

Tutto questo si giudica **solo guardandolo lavorare**: un deploy e un ciclo di osservazione (tre messaggi, i loro run, il tasso di rifiuti) dicono più di dieci misure preventive. Il mio consiglio: **push dei cinque commit, installazione da Lisa, e una sola osservazione** — con la lista già pronta di cosa guardare. Le tre decisioni sopra le prendiamo adesso, così il giro successivo non ha altre domande.

Dimmi come vuoi procedere su A9 (migrare o archiviare) e se parto dall'osservazione.

Actually the more useful comparison is the architectural pattern, and Jaymini's page already tells the pattern:
- **AI Teammates with a role**, not a general agent.

That's the opposite of our design: one agent, 45 tools, 5 surfaces, runs/steps/endings/waits/claims/memory, one general loop. Theirs: many narrow roles, each with a small toolset and a 3-step narrative, output to a review queue.

So the honest architectural answer:

Our scheme isn't "overcomplicated" in the abstract — every part maps to a real need (durability, idempotency, one wait, etc.) — but it is **one general-purpose agent trying to drive 45 tools over 5 surfaces with a mid-size model**, and the measurement says the model can't. The complexity is in the *wrong place*: we built an elaborate harness around a model that can't read the catalogue, instead of narrowing what it has to do.

Concrete proposal (new optics):
1. **Role-scoped agents, not one catalogue.** Split the 45 tools into 4–6 roles with 5–8 tools each (like Jaymini's teammates): filing/mail triage, calendar, files/KB, chat answering. Each role gets its own tiny catalogue, its own instruction, its own budget. The model never sees 45 definitions.
2. **A task, not a run/step machine.** The run document is good and should stay (it's the audit trail), but the *loop* should be a fixed pipeline per role (read → decide → act → report), with the model choosing only among that role's few tools. Branching plans and 20-step budgets are what produce 34-entry plans and 300 s runs.
3. **Review queue instead of silent completion.** Outputs wait for a yes — that's what removes the "done without work" class entirely: the *product* checks, not the model's claim.
4. **Approval as a first-class step** (they have it: "Nothing leaves without you").
5. **A small, visible step narrative** (3 steps) — the UI we just built (about + steps live) is right; it's the *content* that must become a task list, not a plan graph.
6. **Fewer surfaces initially**: mail + files first, not 5.

Also honest: their product is not live (no real connections), so it's a positioning site, not proof. The "proof" is the pattern's simplicity, not their reliability.

And the second honest point: we can't judge our harness without a reliable model. DeepSeek with 45 tools is the weak link; even with the catalogue lines, expect a high refusal rate. Options: (a) narrow the catalogue per role (structural fix), (b) use a stronger model, (c) both.

Recommendation: keep the durability layer (runs, claim, cursors — it's what makes it a product), **replace the "one agent + big catalogue + free-form plan" with role-scoped tasks and a review queue**. Concretely, a staged plan:
- Stage 1 (cheap): cap the catalogue per rule — a rule declares which surfaces it works, and the model gets only those tools (the rule already has a surfaces matrix!). Today `surfaceLines` says what's off, but the catalogue is everything. **The data is already there**: hand `chooseStep` only the tools of the surfaces the run's rule may write + the reading tools. That's a small change with a big effect: a freight rule working chat+files sees ~12 tools, not 45.
- Stage 2: a 3-step task shape instead of branching plans for the common rules; branching stays for the rare ones.
- Stage 3: review queue for outward acts (sends) — replace the "sends: true" licence with a draft that waits for a yes.

That's a real answer to "rethink the approach", grounded in our own evidence, with the first step being cheap and data-justified.

## Cosa fanno quelli che funzionano

**Jaymini** non è un agente: sono **AI Teammates con un ruolo** (Content Writer, Meeting Analyst, Project Coordinator, Researcher…). Ognuno ha **pochi strumenti**, un'istruzione sua, e il lavoro finisce in una **coda di revisione**: «niente esce senza il tuo sì». Quello che l'utente vede sono **tre passi** («letto le note», «trovate 2 decisioni», «bozza scritta») — non un piano a grafo. E le connessioni sono **5 fatte, 25 in arrivo**: partono strette.

I progetti "Jarvis" su GitHub (OpenJarvis, jarvis-ai-assistant, J.A.R.V.I.S. con LangGraph) sono la stessa lezione in piccolo: **assistenti personali con una manciata di tool**, non un ormone generale con quarantacinque.

Avvertenza onesta: Jaymini non è live (nessuna connessione reale), è un sito di posizionamento. Non è la prova che funzionano — è la prova di **come impostano il problema**.

## Sì, il nostro schema è sovradimensionato — ma nel punto sbagliato

Quello che **serve** e va tenuto: il documento del run (è l'audit), il claim, i cursori, un solo wait, gli esiti, la memoria. Sono le cose che rendono un agente un *prodotto* e non una demo.

Quello che è **impalcatura attorno a un modello che non ce la fa**:

- **un catalogo unico da 45 tool** per un pianificatore libero (misura: 260 passi rifiutati su 94 run, 51% dei `done` con un rifiuto, 0 run che chiedono a una persona, piani da 34 voci e 300 s);
- **piani ramificati come forma normale** — il grafo di dipendenze per un lavoro che nel 90% dei casi è «leggi, agisci, riferisci»;
- **`done` come affermazione del modello** invece che come esito verificato dal prodotto;
- **`sends: true` come licenza che il modello vede**: l'invio non dovrebbe mai essere un permesso del prompt, ma una bozza che aspetta un sì.

Il difetto non è la complessità in sé: è che abbiamo messo la complessità **nel modello** (tanti tool, tante superfici, piani liberi) invece che **nel prodotto** (pochi ruoli, pochi tool, revisione).

## La forma nuova, in cinque passi (dal più economico)

1. **Catalogo per ruolo, preso dalla regola.** La regola **dichiara già** le superfici che guarda e su cui scrive. Oggi gliele diciamo in prosa ma gli diamo tutti i 45 tool. Basta passare a `chooseStep` solo i tool delle superfici del run più i lettori: una regola «freight» su chat+files vede ~12 tool, non 45. **È una modifica piccola, il dato esiste già, e la misura punta dritta lì.**
2. **Forma a tre battute.** Un run comune è «leggi → agisci → riferisci»; il grafo di dipendenze resta per le regole che lo chiedono davvero. Spariscono i piani da 34 voci.
3. **Coda di revisione** per gli atti che escono: una mail da mandare è una bozza, e il sì è un passo del prodotto — non una licenza nel prompt. Questo cancella da solo la classe «done senza aver fatto».
4. **Meno superfici all'inizio**: posta + files. Calendario, contatti, KB e chat dopo.
5. **Istruzioni per ruolo** invece di una prosa generale più una per regola.

## Cosa farei adesso

**Il passo 1, e solo quello**, in un commit: è piccolo, reversibile, e il dato che lo giustifica è la regola stessa. Poi **una** osservazione (tre messaggi, rifatti i conti: rifiuti, `done` falsi, run che chiedono) decide se il resto della forma nuova serve o se bastava quello.

Se invece vuoi rivedere l'approccio **davvero da capo** — ruoli al posto dell'agente unico, revisione al posto della chiusura — allora il passo 1 non basta e va scritto come decisione (un ADR che sostituisce 0027/0029/0031 in parte), non come patch.

Dimmi quale delle due: **assottigliare ora e osservare**, oppure **ridisegnare i ruoli** prima di toccare altro.

*Note: Much of the tooling landscape described in this post has changed since December 2024\. For our current approach, see [**how we built Claude Managed Agents**](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents)* *and the [**Managed Agents documentation**.](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview)*  
  
Over the past year, we've worked with dozens of teams building large language model (LLM) agents across industries. Consistently, the most successful implementations weren't using complex frameworks or specialized libraries. Instead, they were building with simple, composable patterns.

In this post, we share what we’ve learned from working with our customers and building agents ourselves, and give practical advice for developers on building effective agents.

## What are agents?

"Agent" can be defined in several ways. Some customers define agents as fully autonomous systems that operate independently over extended periods, using various tools to accomplish complex tasks. Others use the term to describe more prescriptive implementations that follow predefined workflows. At Anthropic, we categorize all these variations as **agentic systems**, but draw an important architectural distinction between **workflows** and **agents** :

- **Workflows** are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths.

- **Agents**, on the other hand, are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks.

Below, we will explore both types of agentic systems in detail. In Appendix 1 (“Agents in Practice”), we describe two domains where customers have found particular value in using these kinds of systems.

## When (and when not) to use agents

When building applications with LLMs, we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed. This might mean not building agentic systems at all. Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and you should consider when this tradeoff makes sense.

When more complexity is warranted, workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, whereas agents are the better option when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed at scale. For many applications, however, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough.

## When and how to use frameworks

There are many frameworks that make agentic systems easier to implement, including:

- The [Claude Agent SDK](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview);

- [Strands Agents SDK by AWS](https://strandsagents.com/latest/);

- [Rivet](https://rivet.ironcladapp.com/), a drag and drop GUI LLM workflow builder; and

- [Vellum](https://www.vellum.ai/), another GUI tool for building and testing complex workflows.

These frameworks make it easy to get started by simplifying standard low-level tasks like calling LLMs, defining and parsing tools, and chaining calls together. However, they often create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts ​​and responses, making them harder to debug. They can also make it tempting to add complexity when a simpler setup would suffice.

We suggest that developers start by using LLM APIs directly: many patterns can be implemented in a few lines of code. If you do use a framework, ensure you understand the underlying code. Incorrect assumptions about what's under the hood are a common source of customer error.

See our [cookbook](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/patterns-agents-basic-workflows) for some sample implementations.

## Building blocks, workflows, and agents

In this section, we’ll explore the common patterns for agentic systems we’ve seen in production. We'll start with our foundational building block—the augmented LLM—and progressively increase complexity, from simple compositional workflows to autonomous agents.

### Building block: The augmented LLM

The basic building block of agentic systems is an LLM enhanced with augmentations such as retrieval, tools, and memory. Our current models can actively use these capabilities—generating their own search queries, selecting appropriate tools, and determining what information to retain.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2Fd3083d3f40bb2b6f477901cc9a240738d3dd1371-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

The augmented LLM

We recommend focusing on two key aspects of the implementation: tailoring these capabilities to your specific use case and ensuring they provide an easy, well-documented interface for your LLM. While there are many ways to implement these augmentations, one approach is through our recently released [Model Context Protocol](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol), which allows developers to integrate with a growing ecosystem of third-party tools with a simple [client implementation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/tutorials/building-a-client#building-mcp-clients).

For the remainder of this post, we'll assume each LLM call has access to these augmented capabilities.

### Workflow: Prompt chaining

Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a sequence of steps, where each LLM call processes the output of the previous one. You can add programmatic checks (see "gate” in the diagram below) on any intermediate steps to ensure that the process is still on track.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F7418719e3dab222dccb379b8879e1dc08ad34c78-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

The prompt chaining workflow

**When to use this workflow:** This workflow is ideal for situations where the task can be easily and cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks. The main goal is to trade off latency for higher accuracy, by making each LLM call an easier task.

**Examples where prompt chaining is useful:**

- Generating Marketing copy, then translating it into a different language.

- Writing an outline of a document, checking that the outline meets certain criteria, then writing the document based on the outline.

### Workflow: Routing

Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task. This workflow allows for separation of concerns, and building more specialized prompts. Without this workflow, optimizing for one kind of input can hurt performance on other inputs.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F5c0c0e9fe4def0b584c04d37849941da55e5e71c-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

The routing workflow

**When to use this workflow:** Routing works well for complex tasks where there are distinct categories that are better handled separately, and where classification can be handled accurately, either by an LLM or a more traditional classification model/algorithm.

**Examples where routing is useful:**

- Directing different types of customer service queries (general questions, refund requests, technical support) into different downstream processes, prompts, and tools.

- Routing easy/common questions to smaller, cost-efficient models like Claude Haiku 4\.5 and hard/unusual questions to more capable models like Claude Sonnet 4\.5 to optimize for best performance.

### Workflow: Parallelization

LLMs can sometimes work simultaneously on a task and have their outputs aggregated programmatically. This workflow, parallelization, manifests in two key variations:

- **Sectioning**: Breaking a task into independent subtasks run in parallel.

- **Voting:** Running the same task multiple times to get diverse outputs.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F406bb032ca007fd1624f261af717d70e6ca86286-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

The parallelization workflow

**When to use this workflow:** Parallelization is effective when the divided subtasks can be parallelized for speed, or when multiple perspectives or attempts are needed for higher confidence results. For complex tasks with multiple considerations, LLMs generally perform better when each consideration is handled by a separate LLM call, allowing focused attention on each specific aspect.

**Examples where parallelization is useful:**

- **Sectioning**:

  - Implementing guardrails where one model instance processes user queries while another screens them for inappropriate content or requests. This tends to perform better than having the same LLM call handle both guardrails and the core response.

  - Automating evals for evaluating LLM performance, where each LLM call evaluates a different aspect of the model’s performance on a given prompt.

- **Voting**:

  - Reviewing a piece of code for vulnerabilities, where several different prompts review and flag the code if they find a problem.

  - Evaluating whether a given piece of content is inappropriate, with multiple prompts evaluating different aspects or requiring different vote thresholds to balance false positives and negatives.

### Workflow: Orchestrator-workers

In the orchestrator-workers workflow, a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F8985fc683fae4780fb34eab1365ab78c7e51bc8e-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

The orchestrator-workers workflow

**When to use this workflow:** This workflow is well-suited for complex tasks where you can’t predict the subtasks needed (in coding, for example, the number of files that need to be changed and the nature of the change in each file likely depend on the task). Whereas it’s topographically similar, the key difference from parallelization is its flexibility—subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input.

**Example where orchestrator-workers is useful:**

- Coding products that make complex changes to multiple files each time.

- Search tasks that involve gathering and analyzing information from multiple sources for possible relevant information.

### Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer

In the evaluator-optimizer workflow, one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F14f51e6406ccb29e695da48b17017e899a6119c7-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

The evaluator-optimizer workflow

**When to use this workflow:** This workflow is particularly effective when we have clear evaluation criteria, and when iterative refinement provides measurable value. The two signs of good fit are, first, that LLM responses can be demonstrably improved when a human articulates their feedback; and second, that the LLM can provide such feedback. This is analogous to the iterative writing process a human writer might go through when producing a polished document.

**Examples where evaluator-optimizer is useful:**

- Literary translation where there are nuances that the translator LLM might not capture initially, but where an evaluator LLM can provide useful critiques.

- Complex search tasks that require multiple rounds of searching and analysis to gather comprehensive information, where the evaluator decides whether further searches are warranted.

### Agents

Agents are emerging in production as LLMs mature in key capabilities—understanding complex inputs, engaging in reasoning and planning, using tools reliably, and recovering from errors. Agents begin their work with either a command from, or interactive discussion with, the human user. Once the task is clear, agents plan and operate independently, potentially returning to the human for further information or judgement. During execution, it's crucial for the agents to gain “ground truth” from the environment at each step (such as tool call results or code execution) to assess its progress. Agents can then pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers. The task often terminates upon completion, but it’s also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control.

Agents can handle sophisticated tasks, but their implementation is often straightforward. They are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop. It is therefore crucial to design toolsets and their documentation clearly and thoughtfully. We expand on best practices for tool development in Appendix 2 ("Prompt Engineering your Tools").

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F58d9f10c985c4eb5d53798dea315f7bb5ab6249e-2401x1000.png&w=3840&q=75)

Autonomous agent

**When to use agents:** Agents can be used for open-ended problems where it’s difficult or impossible to predict the required number of steps, and where you can’t hardcode a fixed path. The LLM will potentially operate for many turns, and you must have some level of trust in its decision-making. Agents' autonomy makes them ideal for scaling tasks in trusted environments.

The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors. We recommend extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with the appropriate guardrails.

**Examples where agents are useful:**

The following examples are from our own implementations:

- A coding Agent to resolve [SWE-bench tasks](https://www.anthropic.com/research/swe-bench-sonnet), which involve edits to many files based on a task description;

- Our [“computer use” reference implementation](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-quickstarts/tree/main/computer-use-demo), where Claude uses a computer to accomplish tasks.

![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F4b9a1f4eb63d5962a6e1746ac26bbc857cf3474f-2400x1666.png&w=3840&q=75)

High-level flow of a coding agent

## Combining and customizing these patterns

These building blocks aren't prescriptive. They're common patterns that developers can shape and combine to fit different use cases. The key to success, as with any LLM features, is measuring performance and iterating on implementations. To repeat: you should consider adding complexity *only* when it demonstrably improves outcomes.

## Summary

Success in the LLM space isn't about building the most sophisticated system. It's about building the *right* system for your needs. Start with simple prompts, optimize them with comprehensive evaluation, and add multi-step agentic systems only when simpler solutions fall short.

When implementing agents, we try to follow three core principles:

1. Maintain **simplicity** in your agent's design.

2. Prioritize **transparency** by explicitly showing the agent’s planning steps.

3. Carefully craft your agent-computer interface (ACI) through thorough tool **documentation and testing**.

Frameworks can help you get started quickly, but don't hesitate to reduce abstraction layers and build with basic components as you move to production. By following these principles, you can create agents that are not only powerful but also reliable, maintainable, and trusted by their users.

## Appendix 1: Agents in practice

Our work with customers has revealed two particularly promising applications for AI agents that demonstrate the practical value of the patterns discussed above. Both applications illustrate how agents add the most value for tasks that require both conversation and action, have clear success criteria, enable feedback loops, and integrate meaningful human oversight.

### A. Customer support

Customer support combines familiar chatbot interfaces with enhanced capabilities through tool integration. This is a natural fit for more open-ended agents because:

- Support interactions naturally follow a conversation flow while requiring access to external information and actions;

- Tools can be integrated to pull customer data, order history, and knowledge base articles;

- Actions such as issuing refunds or updating tickets can be handled programmatically; and

- Success can be clearly measured through user-defined resolutions.

Several companies have demonstrated the viability of this approach through usage-based pricing models that charge only for successful resolutions, showing confidence in their agents' effectiveness.

### B. Coding agents

The software development space has shown remarkable potential for LLM features, with capabilities evolving from code completion to autonomous problem-solving. Agents are particularly effective because:

- Code solutions are verifiable through automated tests;

- Agents can iterate on solutions using test results as feedback;

- The problem space is well-defined and structured; and

- Output quality can be measured objectively.

In our own implementation, agents can now solve real GitHub issues in the [SWE-bench Verified](https://www.anthropic.com/research/swe-bench-sonnet) benchmark based on the pull request description alone. However, whereas automated testing helps verify functionality, human review remains crucial for ensuring solutions align with broader system requirements.

## Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools

No matter which agentic system you're building, tools will likely be an important part of your agent. [Tools](https://www.anthropic.com/news/tool-use-ga) enable Claude to interact with external services and APIs by specifying their exact structure and definition in our API. When Claude responds, it will include a [tool use block](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use#example-api-response-with-a-tool-use-content-block) in the API response if it plans to invoke a tool. Tool definitions and specifications should be given just as much prompt engineering attention as your overall prompts. In this brief appendix, we describe how to prompt engineer your tools.

There are often several ways to specify the same action. For instance, you can specify a file edit by writing a diff, or by rewriting the entire file. For structured output, you can return code inside markdown or inside JSON. In software engineering, differences like these are cosmetic and can be converted losslessly from one to the other. However, some formats are much more difficult for an LLM to write than others. Writing a diff requires knowing how many lines are changing in the chunk header before the new code is written. Writing code inside JSON (compared to markdown) requires extra escaping of newlines and quotes.

Our suggestions for deciding on tool formats are the following:

- Give the model enough tokens to "think" before it writes itself into a corner.

- Keep the format close to what the model has seen naturally occurring in text on the internet.

- Make sure there's no formatting "overhead" such as having to keep an accurate count of thousands of lines of code, or string-escaping any code it writes.

One rule of thumb is to think about how much effort goes into human-computer interfaces (HCI), and plan to invest just as much effort in creating good *agent*\-computer interfaces (ACI). Here are some thoughts on how to do so:

- Put yourself in the model's shoes. Is it obvious how to use this tool, based on the description and parameters, or would you need to think carefully about it? If so, then it’s probably also true for the model. A good tool definition often includes example usage, edge cases, input format requirements, and clear boundaries from other tools.

- How can you change parameter names or descriptions to make things more obvious? Think of this as writing a great docstring for a junior developer on your team. This is especially important when using many similar tools.

- Test how the model uses your tools: Run many example inputs in our [workbench](https://console.anthropic.com/workbench) to see what mistakes the model makes, and iterate.

- [Poka-yoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poka-yoke) your tools. Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes.

While building our agent for [SWE-bench](https://www.anthropic.com/research/swe-bench-sonnet), we actually spent more time optimizing our tools than the overall prompt. For example, we found that the model would make mistakes with tools using relative filepaths after the agent had moved out of the root directory. To fix this, we changed the tool to always require absolute filepaths—and we found that the model used this method flawlessly.
