# Agent orchestration

Orchestration refers to the flow of agents in your app. Which agents run, in what order, and how is the next step decided? There are two main ways to orchestrate agents:

1. Allowing the LLM to make decisions: this uses the intelligence of an LLM to plan, reason, and decide on what steps to take based on that.

2. Orchestrating via code: determining the flow of agents via your code.

You can mix and match these patterns. Each has their own tradeoffs, described below.

## Orchestrating via LLM

An agent is an LLM equipped with instructions, tools and handoffs. This means that given an open-ended task, the LLM can autonomously plan how it will tackle the task, using tools to take actions and acquire data, and using handoffs to delegate tasks to sub-agents. For example, a research agent could be equipped with capabilities like:

- Web search to find information online

- File search and retrieval to search through proprietary data and connected data sources

- Computer use to take actions on a computer

- Code execution to do data analysis

- Handoffs to specialized agents that are great at planning, report writing and more.

### Core SDK patterns

In the Python SDK, two orchestration patterns come up most often:

| Pattern | How it works | Best when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agents as tools | A manager agent keeps control of the conversation and calls specialist agents through `Agent.as_tool()`. | You want one agent to own the final answer, combine outputs from multiple specialists, or enforce shared SDK guardrails in one place. |
| Handoffs | A triage agent routes the conversation to a specialist, and that specialist becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn. | You want the specialist to respond directly, keep prompts focused, or have the handoff switch the active instructions without requiring the manager to narrate the result. |

Use **agents as tools** when a specialist should help with a bounded subtask but should not take over the user-facing conversation. Use **handoffs** when routing itself is part of the workflow and you want the chosen specialist to own the remainder of the current turn.

You can also combine the two. A triage agent might hand off to a specialist, and that specialist can still call other agents as tools for narrow subtasks.

This pattern is great when the task is open-ended and you want to rely on the intelligence of an LLM. The most important tactics here are:

1. Invest in good prompts. Make it clear what tools are available, how to use them, and what constraints the agent must follow.

2. Monitor your app and iterate on it. See where things go wrong, and iterate on your prompts.

3. Allow the agent to introspect and improve. For example, run it in a loop, and let it critique itself; or, provide error messages and let it improve.

4. Have specialized agents that excel in one task, rather than having a general purpose agent that is expected to be good at anything.

5. Invest in [evals](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/evals). This lets you train your agents to improve and get better at tasks.

If you want the core SDK primitives behind this style of orchestration, start with [tools](../tools/), [handoffs](../handoffs/), and [running agents](../running_agents/).

## Orchestrating via code

While orchestrating via LLM is powerful, orchestrating via code makes tasks more deterministic and predictable, in terms of speed, cost and performance. Common patterns here are:

- Using [structured outputs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs) to generate well formed data that you can inspect with your code. For example, you might ask an agent to classify the task into a few categories, and then pick the next agent based on the category.

- Chaining multiple agents by transforming the output of one into the input of the next. You can decompose a task like writing a blog post into a series of steps \- do research, write an outline, write the blog post, critique it, and then improve it.

- In each iteration of a `while` loop, run the task agent to produce an output, then run an evaluator agent to assess that output and provide feedback; stop when the evaluator says the output passes the required criteria.

- Running multiple agents in parallel, e.g. via Python primitives like `asyncio.gather`. This is useful for speed when you have multiple tasks that don't depend on each other.

We have a number of examples in [`examples/agent_patterns`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples/agent_patterns).

## Related guides

- [Agents](../agents/) for composition patterns and agent configuration.

- [Tools](../tools/#agents-as-tools) for `Agent.as_tool()` and manager-style orchestration.

- [Handoffs](../handoffs/) for delegation between specialist agents.

- [Running agents](../running_agents/) for per-run orchestration controls and conversation state.

- [Quickstart](../quickstart/) for a minimal end-to-end handoff example.

# Guardrails

Guardrails enable you to do checks and validations of user input and agent output. For example, imagine you have an agent that uses a very smart (and hence slow/expensive) model to help with customer requests. You wouldn't want malicious users to ask the model to help them with their math homework. So, you can run a guardrail with a fast/cheap model. If the guardrail detects malicious usage, it can immediately raise an error, saving time and money. Blocking execution guarantees that the expensive model does not start; with parallel execution, the expensive model may already have started before the guardrail completes. See "Execution modes" below for details.

There are two kinds of guardrails:

1. Input guardrails run on the initial user input

2. Output guardrails run on the final agent output

## Workflow boundaries

Guardrails are attached to agents and tools, but they do not all run at the same points in a workflow:

- **Input guardrails** run only for the first agent in the chain.

- **Output guardrails** run only for the agent that produces the final output.

- **Tool guardrails** run on every guarded function-tool invocation, including local MCP tools when their server configures guardrails, with input guardrails before execution and output guardrails after execution.

If you need checks before and/or after each custom function-tool call in a workflow that includes managers, handoffs, or delegated specialists, use tool guardrails instead of relying only on agent-level input/output guardrails.

## Input guardrails

A guardrail can call an external classifier directly; it does not need to run another agent. For a native OpenAI Decisions client example, see [Decisions API](../models/#decisions-api).

Input guardrails run in 3 steps:

1. First, the guardrail receives the same input passed to the agent.

2. Next, the guardrail function runs to produce a [`GuardrailFunctionOutput`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.GuardrailFunctionOutput "GuardrailFunctionOutput dataclass"), which is then wrapped in an [`InputGuardrailResult`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.InputGuardrailResult "InputGuardrailResult dataclass")

3. Finally, we check if [`.tripwire_triggered`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.GuardrailFunctionOutput.tripwire_triggered "tripwire_triggered instance-attribute") is true. If true, an [`InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`](../ref/exceptions/#agents.exceptions.InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered "InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered") exception is raised, so you can appropriately respond to the user or handle the exception.

Note

Input guardrails are intended to run on user input, so an agent's guardrails only run if the agent is the *first* agent. You might wonder, why is the `guardrails` property on the agent instead of passed to `Runner.run`? It's because guardrails tend to be related to the actual Agent \- you'd run different guardrails for different agents, so colocating the code is useful for readability.

### Execution modes

Input guardrails support two execution modes:

- **Parallel execution** (default, `run_in_parallel=True`): The guardrail runs concurrently with the agent's execution. This provides the best latency since both start at the same time. However, if the guardrail's tripwire is triggered, the agent may have already consumed tokens and executed tools before being cancelled.

- **Blocking execution** (`run_in_parallel=False`): The guardrail runs and completes *before* the agent starts. If the guardrail tripwire is triggered, the agent never executes, preventing token consumption and tool execution. This is ideal for cost optimization and when you want to avoid potential side effects from tool calls.

## Output guardrails

Output guardrails run in 3 steps:

1. First, the guardrail receives the output produced by the agent.

2. Next, the guardrail function runs to produce a [`GuardrailFunctionOutput`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.GuardrailFunctionOutput "GuardrailFunctionOutput dataclass"), which is then wrapped in an [`OutputGuardrailResult`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.OutputGuardrailResult "OutputGuardrailResult dataclass")

3. Finally, we check if [`.tripwire_triggered`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.GuardrailFunctionOutput.tripwire_triggered "tripwire_triggered instance-attribute") is true. If true, an [`OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`](../ref/exceptions/#agents.exceptions.OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered "OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered") exception is raised, so you can appropriately respond to the user or handle the exception.

Note

Output guardrails are intended to run on the final agent output, so an agent's guardrails only run if the agent is the *last* agent. Similar to the input guardrails, we do this because guardrails tend to be related to the actual Agent \- you'd run different guardrails for different agents, so colocating the code is useful for readability.

Output guardrails always run after the agent completes, so they don't support the `run_in_parallel` parameter.

An output tripwire and an exception raised by the guardrail function have different session behavior. A tripwire rejects the candidate final output. When a tripwire fires, the runner asks the configured session to persist already-completed tool call and tool output items, together with any reasoning context required to replay those calls, while excluding the rejected candidate final output. The runner applies this tripwire rule to both streaming and non-streaming runs. When the guardrail function raises an exception instead of returning a tripwire result, the runner treats the verdict as unknown and asks the configured session to persist the completed final-turn items before surfacing the guardrail exception. If that session write also fails, the session write error takes precedence. Streaming runs use the same persistence ordering as non-streaming runs and raise the terminal exception from `stream_events()`. An immediate [`RunResultStreaming.cancel()`](../ref/result/#agents.result.RunResultStreaming.cancel "cancel") call while the output guardrail is running cancels the in-flight guardrail and does not start a final-turn session write.

Terminal function-tool output needs additional handling because the tool has already run before the agent-level output guardrail checks the value. When [`Agent.tool_use_behavior`](../ref/agent/#agents.agent.Agent.tool_use_behavior "tool_use_behavior class-attribute instance-attribute") makes that tool result the final output and an output tripwire rejects it, the SDK retains a replay-valid function call/output pair only when it can rebuild the pair from validated fields. The retained `function_call_output` payload is replaced with the default text `"Output withheld by an output guardrail."`; the original tool-output payload is not retained in the session, `RunState`, streamed result state, or sandbox memory input. The SDK does retain validated function-call metadata required for replay, including the function arguments, so that metadata can contain data that also appeared in the rejected output. Current-response [`OutputGuardrailResult`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.OutputGuardrailResult "OutputGuardrailResult dataclass") objects also replace `agent_output` with the resolved placeholder and clear `output_info`. Current-response [`ToolOutputGuardrailResult`](../ref/tool_guardrails/#agents.tool_guardrails.ToolOutputGuardrailResult "ToolOutputGuardrailResult dataclass") objects preserve the allow/reject behavior type but replace payload-bearing `output_info` and rejection messages with the same placeholder. Earlier accepted turns and guardrail results remain unchanged. If the response contains reasoning or another shape that the SDK cannot sanitize safely, the SDK discards the complete current-response suffix instead of retaining the rejected output payload. A guardrail function that raises an exception has not returned a rejection verdict, so the completed terminal-tool turn follows the exception persistence behavior described above.

Set [`RunConfig.output_guardrail_blocked_message`](../ref/run/#agents.run.RunConfig.output_guardrail_blocked_message "output_guardrail_blocked_message class-attribute instance-attribute") to a non-empty string or a synchronous formatter when your application needs a different data-free placeholder. The formatter receives [`OutputGuardrailBlockedMessageArgs`](../ref/run_config/#agents.run_config.OutputGuardrailBlockedMessageArgs "OutputGuardrailBlockedMessageArgs dataclass") with the SDK default, the guardrail name, the agent, and the active run context. It never receives the rejected tool output or guardrail `output_info`. The returned text is persisted and replayed wherever the SDK retains the sanitized terminal-tool turn, so keep it free of sensitive data and do not copy secrets from the run context. If the formatter raises, returns `None`, returns an empty or non-string value, or produces an awaitable, the SDK uses the default placeholder. Async formatter functions are rejected when `RunConfig` is constructed.

```
from agents import OutputGuardrailBlockedMessageArgs, RunConfig


def blocked_message(args: OutputGuardrailBlockedMessageArgs[dict[str, str]]) -> str:
    return f"Output blocked by policy: {args.guardrail_name}."


run_config = RunConfig(output_guardrail_blocked_message=blocked_message)
```

## Tool guardrails

Tool guardrails wrap **`FunctionTool` instances** and let you validate or block calls to those tools before and after execution. They are configured on the tool itself and run every time that tool is invoked.

- Input tool guardrails run before the tool executes and can skip the call, replace the output with a message, or raise a tripwire.

- Output tool guardrails run after the tool executes and can replace the output or raise a tripwire.

- If a function tool requires approval, input tool guardrails normally run after approval and immediately before execution. Set [`RunConfig.tool_execution`](../ref/run/#agents.run.RunConfig.tool_execution "tool_execution class-attribute instance-attribute") to [`ToolExecutionConfig(pre_approval_tool_input_guardrails=True)`](../ref/run_config/#agents.run_config.ToolExecutionConfig "ToolExecutionConfig dataclass") when you want those input checks to run before the pending approval interruption is emitted. Calls that pass this pre-approval check are still checked again after approval before the tool executes.

- Tool guardrails use the `FunctionTool` execution pipeline. You can attach them directly to a custom tool created with `tool` or [`function_tool`](../ref/tool/#agents.tool.function_tool "function_tool"). You can also set `tool_input_guardrails` and `tool_output_guardrails` on a local MCP server; the SDK attaches those lists to every tool exposed by that server. Handoffs run through the SDK's handoff pipeline rather than the function-tool pipeline, so tool guardrails do not apply to the handoff call itself. Hosted tools (`WebSearchTool`, `FileSearchTool`, `HostedMCPTool`, `CodeInterpreterTool`, `ImageGenerationTool`) and built-in execution tools (`ComputerTool`, `ShellTool`, `ApplyPatchTool`, `LocalShellTool`) do not use this guardrail pipeline, and [`Agent.as_tool()`](../ref/agent/#agents.agent.Agent.as_tool "as_tool") does not currently expose tool-guardrail options directly. See [MCP server tool guardrails](../mcp/#tool-guardrails) for the local MCP configuration.

See the code snippet below for details.

## Tripwires

If an agent input or output fails a guardrail, the guardrail can signal this with a tripwire. The runner immediately raises an `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` or `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` exception and halts agent execution. Tool guardrails use the corresponding `ToolInputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` and `ToolOutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` exceptions.

For agent-level tripwires, the exception's `guardrail_result` identifies the guardrail that triggered the tripwire. For an input tripwire raised by the runner, `exception.run_data.input_guardrail_results` contains every input guardrail result completed before the run stopped, including the result that triggered the tripwire. Output tripwires provide the equivalent accumulated results through `exception.run_data.output_guardrail_results`.

Tool tripwire exceptions instead expose the triggering `guardrail` and `output` directly. Their `run_data.tool_input_guardrail_results` and `run_data.tool_output_guardrail_results` lists preserve results accumulated from completed turns before the failure; the triggering result is available through the exception's `output`. Other runner-managed failures, such as `MaxTurnsExceeded`, also preserve completed tool guardrail results in these lists. After `stream_events()` raises an exception, the streamed result exposes the same accumulated agent and tool guardrail result lists. `run_data` can be `None` when an exception is raised outside a runner-managed execution path.

## Implementing a guardrail

You need to provide a function that receives input, and returns a [`GuardrailFunctionOutput`](../ref/guardrail/#agents.guardrail.GuardrailFunctionOutput "GuardrailFunctionOutput dataclass"). In this example, we'll do this by running an Agent under the hood.

```
from pydantic import BaseModel
from agents import (
    Agent,
    GuardrailFunctionOutput,
    InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered,
    RunContextWrapper,
    Runner,
    TResponseInputItem,
)
from agents.decorators import input_guardrail


class MathHomeworkOutput(BaseModel):
    is_math_homework: bool
    reasoning: str


guardrail_agent = Agent(  # (1)!
    name="Guardrail check",
    instructions="Check if the user is asking you to do their math homework.",
    output_type=MathHomeworkOutput,
)


@input_guardrail
async def math_guardrail(  # (2)!
    ctx: RunContextWrapper[None], agent: Agent, input: str | list[TResponseInputItem]
) -> GuardrailFunctionOutput:
    result = await Runner.run(guardrail_agent, input, context=ctx.context)

    return GuardrailFunctionOutput(
        output_info=result.final_output,  # (3)!
        tripwire_triggered=result.final_output.is_math_homework,
    )


agent = Agent(  # (4)!
    name="Customer support agent",
    instructions="You are a customer support agent. You help customers with their questions.",
    input_guardrails=[math_guardrail],
)


async def main():
    # This should trip the guardrail
    try:
        await Runner.run(agent, "Hello, can you help me solve for x: 2x + 3 = 11?")
        print("Guardrail didn't trip - this is unexpected")

    except InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered:
        print("Math homework guardrail tripped")
```

1. We'll use this agent in our guardrail function.

2. This is the guardrail function that receives the agent's input/context, and returns the result.

3. We can include extra information in the guardrail result.

4. This is the actual agent that defines the workflow.

Output guardrails are similar.

```
from pydantic import BaseModel
from agents import (
    Agent,
    GuardrailFunctionOutput,
    OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered,
    RunContextWrapper,
    Runner,
)
from agents.decorators import output_guardrail


class MessageOutput(BaseModel):  # (1)!
    response: str


class MathOutput(BaseModel):  # (2)!
    reasoning: str
    is_math: bool


guardrail_agent = Agent(
    name="Guardrail check",
    instructions="Check if the output includes any math.",
    output_type=MathOutput,
)


@output_guardrail
async def math_guardrail(  # (3)!
    ctx: RunContextWrapper, agent: Agent, output: MessageOutput
) -> GuardrailFunctionOutput:
    result = await Runner.run(guardrail_agent, output.response, context=ctx.context)

    return GuardrailFunctionOutput(
        output_info=result.final_output,
        tripwire_triggered=result.final_output.is_math,
    )


agent = Agent(  # (4)!
    name="Customer support agent",
    instructions="You are a customer support agent. You help customers with their questions.",
    output_guardrails=[math_guardrail],
    output_type=MessageOutput,
)


async def main():
    # This should trip the guardrail
    try:
        await Runner.run(agent, "Hello, can you help me solve for x: 2x + 3 = 11?")
        print("Guardrail didn't trip - this is unexpected")

    except OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered:
        print("Math output guardrail tripped")
```

1. This is the actual agent's output type.

2. This is the guardrail's output type.

3. This is the guardrail function that receives the agent's output, and returns the result.

4. This is the actual agent that defines the workflow.

Lastly, here are examples of tool guardrails.

```
import json
from agents import (
    Agent,
    Runner,
    ToolGuardrailFunctionOutput,
)
from agents.decorators import tool, tool_input_guardrail, tool_output_guardrail


@tool_input_guardrail
def block_secrets(data):
    args = json.loads(data.context.tool_arguments or "{}")
    if "sk-" in json.dumps(args):
        return ToolGuardrailFunctionOutput.reject_content(
            "Remove secrets before calling this tool."
        )
    return ToolGuardrailFunctionOutput.allow()


@tool_output_guardrail
def redact_output(data):
    text = str(data.output or "")
    if "sk-" in text:
        return ToolGuardrailFunctionOutput.reject_content("Output contained sensitive data.")
    return ToolGuardrailFunctionOutput.allow()


@tool(
    tool_input_guardrails=[block_secrets],
    tool_output_guardrails=[redact_output],
)
def classify_text(text: str) -> str:
    """Classify text for internal routing."""
    return f"length:{len(text)}"


agent = Agent(name="Classifier", tools=[classify_text])
result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "hello world")
print(result.final_output)
```

{"content":"/**\n * The agent's areas — ADR 0038.\n *\n * Each area is a module of tools with one concern: posta, files, calendario,\n * contatti, conoscenza, workorder, chat, memoria. A run is handed **the areas its\n * change and its instruction declare**, plus the three that every run needs —\n * chat (the interface), conoscenza (the shared library) and memoria (what the\n * installation knows).\n *\n * This file is the one place that says which area a tool belongs to: a new tool\n * names its area here, and nothing else in the tree repeats the mapping. The\n * catalogue a turn sees is computed from it, so the model never again reads\n * forty-five names to use four.\n */\n\n/** The areas the agent works in. */\nexport const AREA_NAMES = [\n  \"mail\",\n  \"files\",\n  \"calendar\",\n  \"contacts\",\n  \"knowledge\",\n  \"workorders\",\n  \"chat\",\n  \"memory\",\n] as const;\n\nexport type AreaName = (typeof AREA_NAMES)[number];\n\n/**\n * How many areas one group's instruction may declare.\n *\n * Three is the ceiling that keeps a turn's catalogue small: an instruction that\n * names five is thirty tools in one answer, which is the failure ADR 0038 exists\n * to undo. A group that needs more writes two instructions' worth of work as two\n * groups, or narrows the one it has.\n */\nexport const MAX_DECLARED_AREAS = 3;\n\n/** The areas every run gets, whatever its change and instruction say. */\nexport const TRANSVERSAL_AREAS: readonly AreaName[] = [\"chat\", \"knowledge\", \"memory\"];\n\n/**\n * The area a tool belongs to, from its name's own prefix.\n *\n * A tool's name is `area.action` by construction (the catalogue's naming rule),\n * so the mapping is read and not maintained twice. A name that matches no area is\n * a defect in the tool, and it is refused here rather than silently handed to\n * every run.\n */\nexport function areaOf(toolName: string): AreaName {\n  const prefix = toolName.split(\".\")[0] ?? \"\";\n  const found = AREA_NAMES.find((area) => area === prefix);\n  if (!found)\n    throw new Error(\n      `The tool \"${toolName}\" names no area: its name must start with one of ${AREA_NAMES.join(\", \")}.`,\n    );\n  return found;\n}\n\n/**\n * What a group declares, or the sentence that refuses it.\n *\n * The declared areas are what an instruction states its group works; a change\n * that lands in an area nobody declared is still worked if its own area is the\n * change's (the change is the trigger, ADR 0038) — this is the ceiling, not the\n * routing.\n */\nexport function declaredAreas(areas: readonly string[]): {\n  areas: readonly AreaName[];\n  problem: string | null;\n} {\n  const known = areas.filter((one): one is AreaName =>\n    (AREA_NAMES as readonly string[]).includes(one),\n  );\n  const unknown = areas.filter((one) => !(AREA_NAMES as readonly string[]).includes(one));\n  if (unknown.length)\n    return {\n      areas: known,\n      problem: `There is no area called ${unknown.map((one) => `\"${one}\"`).join(\", \")}. The areas are: ${AREA_NAMES.join(\", \")}.`,\n    };\n  if (known.length > MAX_DECLARED_AREAS)\n    return {\n      areas: known,\n      problem: `An instruction may declare at most ${MAX_DECLARED_AREAS} areas, and this one declares ${known.length}: ${known.join(\", \")}. Split the work into two groups, or narrow what this one does.`,\n    };\n  return { areas: known, problem: null };\n}\n\n/**\n * The areas one run may use: its change's, its instruction's, and the transversal\n * three. Ordered, deduplicated, and never empty.\n */\nexport function selectAreas(\n  change: AreaName,\n  declared: readonly AreaName[],\n): readonly AreaName[] {\n  const held = new Set<AreaName>([change, ...declared, ...TRANSVERSAL_AREAS]);\n  return AREA_NAMES.filter((area) => held.has(area));\n}\n","path":"/home/remote/git/gilbert/server/src/agent/areas.ts"}

/**
 * The surfaces of a group's own account, and what a rule may do on each
 * (ADR 0031).
 *
 * One definition for both tiers: the rule's parser and guard read it, the run
 * document carries it, and the Administration editor draws it. A mode is not an
 * authority class (ADR 0028): it says **where** a run may act, never that a
 * destructive act needs no person's word.
 *
 * - `off`: no wake, no write. Reading stays free — a reading is proof, not an
 *   act.
 * - `watch`: the surface wakes the rule, and the rule may write it inside the
 *   run that wake opened.
 * - `ondemand`: the surface never wakes the rule; an open run may write it.
 *
 * Chat is always `watch`: the conversation is where the group calls the agent
 * and where its report is written.
 */

export type SurfaceMode = "off" | "watch" | "ondemand";

/** Every surface a rule's matrix names, in the order the editor draws them. */
export type SurfaceName =
  | "chat"
  | "mail"
  | "files"
  | "knowledge"
  | "workorder"
  | "calendar";

/** The surfaces in the editor's order. */
export const SURFACES: readonly SurfaceName[] = [
  "chat",
  "mail",
  "files",
  "knowledge",
  "workorder",
  "calendar",
];

 * The half of a catalogue that cannot change anything: the tools that write
 * nothing.
 *
 * This is the whole of what makes a writing tool unreachable while reading: the
 * caller is handed the write-free half, so a tool that writes is not in it to

/** A surface list a test asks a rule to watch. */
type WatchList = Array<keyof RuleDoc["surfaces"]>;

/** A rule this build writes, watching one surface, removed with its test. */
async function putRule(id: string, watches: WatchList = ["mail"]): Promise<void> {
  await createRule(ctx, accountId, rule(id, watches));
  written.push(id);
}

/** A rule this build writes, watching the surfaces named and on demand elsewhere. */
function rule(id: string, watches: WatchList = ["mail"]): RuleDoc {
  const surfaces: RuleDoc["surfaces"] = {
    chat: "watch",
    mail: "ondemand",
    files: "ondemand",
    knowledge: "ondemand",
    workorder: "ondemand",
    calendar: "ondemand",
  };
  for (const surface of watches) surfaces[surface] = "watch";
  surfaces.chat = "watch";
  return {
    v: RULE_VERSION,
    id,
    surfaces,
    instruction: "Answer the shipper within the day.",
    sends: false,
  };
}

/** The inbox id of an account, read from the server: mailbox ids are its own. */
async function inboxOf(account: string): Promise<string> {
  const boxes = await clientOf(ctx).call<{
    list?: Array<{ id?: string; role?: string }>;
  }>("Mailbox/get", { accountId: account, ids: null, properties: ["id", "role"] }, [
    CAPABILITIES.mail,
  ]);
  const inbox = (boxes.list ?? []).find((box) => box.role === "inbox")?.id;
  assert.ok(inbox, `the account ${account} has an inbox`);

test("a malformed answer costs a step and is asked again, not the run", async () => {
  /*
   * A model stuck on one malformed answer repeats it, and every repeat is a
   * model call and a step that ended refused — so the run stops on the budget it
   * declares, not on a counter invisible in the record. A live run died after
   * three all-refused rounds with its budget untouched; the person heard nothing,
   * which is the ending this replaced.
   */
  const id = "intake-stuck-model";
  await putRule(id);
  const agent = loop();
  await agent.start();

  answerWith({ rules: [id], facts: {} });
  const stuck = {
    calls: [
      {
        name: "chat.say",
        arguments: { text: "the same malformed answer" },
        needs: { step: "nowhere", when: "done" },
      },
    ],
  };
  answerWith(stuck);
  answerWith(stuck);
  answerWith({ done: "the model recovered and finished" });
  await deliver("a change the model fumbles twice");
  await agent.pass();

  const run = await runOf(id);
  assert.equal(run.state, "done", "two refusals are not an ending");
  assert.equal(
    run.plan.filter((step) => step.state === "failed").length,
    2,
    "both refusals are on the record",
  );
  assert.equal(run.spent.steps, 2, "and each one spent a step of the budget");
  assert.equal(run.ended?.why, "the model recovered and finished");
});

 * where every record puts them: a `Status` under `## Consequences` is a record
 * whose header says nothing, and a reader looking for it does not scroll.
 */
export function recordProblems({ path, text }) {
  const problems = [];
  const headerEnd = FIRST_SECTION.exec(text)?.index ?? text.length;

  for (const [what, pattern, allowed] of [
    ["Status", STATUS_LINE, STATUS_VALUES],
    ["Implementation", IMPLEMENTATION_LINE, IMPLEMENTATION_VALUES],
  ]) {
    const found = [...text.matchAll(pattern)];
    if (found.length === 0) {
      problems.push({ why: `no \`${what}\` line: every record states one` });
      continue;
    }
    if (found.length > 1) {
      problems.push({
        line: lineOf(text, found[1].index),
        why: `${found.length} \`${what}\` lines: a record states one`,
      });
    }
    const [match] = found;
    const line = lineOf(text, match.index);
    if (match.index > headerEnd) {
      problems.push({
        line,
        why: `\`${what}\` is below the record's first section; it belongs in the header`,
      });
    }
    /* The word it begins with, so a value that says nothing is refused: `Built`
       may be followed by a comma or a full stop, which is why this is a word
       boundary rather than a period. */
    const value = match[1].trim();
    if (!allowed.some((word) => new RegExp(`^${word}\\b`).test(value))) {
      problems.push({
        line,
        why: `\`${what}: ${value}\` begins with none of ${allowed.join(", ")}`,
      });
    }
  }
  return problems.map((one) => ({ path, ...one }));
}

/**
 * A group's standing instruction: where it is read from (ADR 0031).
 *
 * The shape, its parser and the document's address are the **shared** tree's
 * (`shared/instruction.ts`), because both tiers name them — the server reads the
 * document here, and a member's client writes it with the group's own session.
 * What lives on this tier is the read: the app folder, the bytes and the refusal.
 */

import { type Ctx, readAppFileAt } from "../appFolder.js";
import { CodedError, errorMessage } from "../shared/errors.js";
import {
  INSTRUCTION_FILE,
  parseInstructionDocumentDetailed,
} from "../shared/instruction.js";

export {
  INSTRUCTION_FILE,
  INSTRUCTION_VERSION,
  type InstructionDoc,
  parseInstructionDocumentDetailed,
} from "../shared/instruction.js";

/**
 * An instruction this build cannot use.
 *
 * One that is there but unreadable is a **defect the agent reports**, never a
 * level it silently drops (ADR 0031): the pass fails with this and the next one
 * tries again, which is how the people it belongs to learn that their instruction
 * stopped being carried. The code is what a surface composes its own sentence
 * from.
 */
export class InstructionError extends CodedError {
  constructor(code: string, message: string, status = 502) {
    super(code, message, status, "InstructionError");
  }
}

/** The group's standing instruction, or null when it has written none. */
export async function readInstruction(
  ctx: Ctx,
  accountId: string,
): Promise<string | null> {
  let found: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof readAppFileAt>>;
  try {
    found = await readAppFileAt(ctx, accountId, INSTRUCTION_FILE);
  } catch (err) {
    // A document that is there with bytes that do not come back is unreadable,
    // not absent: reading it as absent would carry a call with no group level.
    throw unreadable(errorMessage(err));
  }
  if (!found) return null;
  const parsed = parseInstructionDocumentDetailed(found.text);
  if ("problem" in parsed) throw unreadable(parsed.problem);
  return parsed.instruction.instruction;
}

function unreadable(why: string): InstructionError {
  return new InstructionError(
    "instruction_unreadable",
    `The group's instruction at ${INSTRUCTION_FILE} is not readable: ${why} It has been left exactly as it is.`,
  );
}

/**
 * Where a group's rules live, and what a rule's name may be (ADR 0031).
 *
 * A rule is one document named `<id>.json` under `rules/` in the **group's own
 * account** — the group's `gilbert` app folder. The address is here because both
 * tiers name it: the server reads and writes a rule, and a member's client writes
 * one with the group's own session. The shape and its parser are
 * `agent/rule.ts`; where the document is read and written is `agent/rules.ts`.
 */

import { CodedError } from "./errors.js";

/** Where a group's rules live under its app folder: the one path constant. */
export const RULES_DIR = "rules";

/**
 * A rule this build cannot use.
 *
 * A rule that is there but unreadable is a **defect the agent reports**, never a
 * shape it guesses at (ADR 0031): a document that is not the shape this build
 * writes, or whose `id` is not the name it is filed under, is refused with its
 * path and the reason rather than read as a rule with nothing in it — which
 * would be a rule the agent then carries out as though it said nothing. The code
 * is what a surface composes its own sentence from.
 */
export class RuleError extends CodedError {
  constructor(code: string, message: string, status = 502) {
    super(code, message, status, "RuleError");
  }
}

/**
 * A rule's file name inside `rules/`.
 *
 * A rule's id is a file name and nothing else: a member names a rule, and an id
 * carrying a path separator would file it in a folder of its own rather than
 * beside its siblings. `.` and `..` are refused by the same test, and by
 * `pathSegments` after it. A writer that already holds the `rules/` folder names
 * the file with this; a reader of the account walks the path below.
 */
function ruleFileName(id: string): string {
  if (!/^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$/.test(id))
    throw new RuleError(
      "rule_id_invalid",
      `"${id}" is not a rule name: a rule is named by letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, with no spaces.`,
      400,
    );
  return `${id}.json`;
}

/** A rule's document path, app-folder-relative: `rules/` and the file name. */
export function rulePath(id: string): string {
  return `${RULES_DIR}/${ruleFileName(id)}`;
}

/**
 * A group's standing instruction, as a document (ADR 0031).
 *
 * One document per group account: `instruction.json` at the root of that
 * account's `gilbert` app folder, beside the label catalog — the two documents a
 * group owns whole. It says one thing, in prose: how the group wants its agent to
 * work. It is the **middle** of the three levels the model is told, above the
 * rule's own instruction and below the installation's own line.
 *
 * The shape, its parser and the address live here because both tiers name them:
 * the server reads the document, and a member's client writes it with the group's
 * own session. What reads it is `agent/instruction.ts`.
 */

import { errorDetail } from "./errors.js";
import { isRecord } from "./json.js";

/** Where a group's standing instruction lives: the one path constant. */
export const INSTRUCTION_FILE = "instruction.json";

/**
 * The schema this build writes and reads. A document of another version is
 * refused, so a field of the shape below moves this with it — the version is
 * how a change reaches an instruction a group has already written.
 */
export const INSTRUCTION_VERSION = 1;

/** One group's standing instruction, as it is stored. */
export interface InstructionDoc {
  /** The schema version; `INSTRUCTION_VERSION` today. */
  v: 1;
  /** In prose, how the group wants its agent to work. */
  instruction: string;
}

/**
 * Parse one stored instruction.
 *
 * Strict JSON, an object at the top, then the two fields checked: a `v` this
 * build does not know is refused rather than read as though it meant the same,
 * and an instruction that is not text or says nothing is refused rather than
 * carried into a call as a heading over nothing. A key this build does not know
 * is ignored, so a field a later build added decides nothing here.
 */
export function parseInstructionDocumentDetailed(
  raw: string,
): { instruction: InstructionDoc } | { problem: string } {
  let whole: unknown;
  try {
    whole = JSON.parse(raw);
  } catch (err) {
    return { problem: `Not valid JSON${errorDetail(err)}.` };
  }
  if (!isRecord(whole)) return { problem: "The document must be a JSON object." };
  if (whole.v !== INSTRUCTION_VERSION)
    return {
      problem: `"v" is ${JSON.stringify(whole.v)}; this build reads version ${INSTRUCTION_VERSION}.`,
    };
  if (typeof whole.instruction !== "string" || !whole.instruction.trim())
    return { problem: '"instruction" must say how the group wants its agent to work.' };
  return {
    instruction: { v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: whole.instruction },
  };
}

{"content":"/**\n * A group's standing instruction, as a document (ADR 0038).\n *\n * One document per group account: `instruction.json` at the root of that\n * account's `gilbert` app folder, beside the label catalog — the two documents a\n * group owns whole. It says two things: in prose, how the group wants its agent to\n * work, and in the list, **which areas** that work is in.\n *\n * The shape, its parser and the address live here because both tiers name them:\n * the server reads the document and selects a run's catalogue from its areas, and\n * a member's client writes it with the group's own session.\n */\n\nimport { errorDetail } from \"./errors.js\";\nimport { declaredAreas, type AreaName } from \"./areas.js\";\nimport { isRecord } from \"./json.js\";\n\n/** Where a group's standing instruction lives: the one path constant. */\nexport const INSTRUCTION_FILE = \"instruction.json\";\n\n/**\n * The schema this build writes and reads. A document of another version is\n * refused, so a field of the shape below moves this with it — the version is\n * how a change reaches an instruction a group has already written.\n *\n * Version 1 carried the prose alone; it is still read, and upgraded in memory,\n * because an installation wrote one before the areas existed.\n */\nexport const INSTRUCTION_VERSION = 2;\n\n/** One group's standing instruction, as it is stored. */\nexport interface InstructionDoc {\n  /** The schema version; `INSTRUCTION_VERSION` today. */\n  v: 2;\n  /** In prose, how the group wants its agent to work. */\n  instruction: string;\n  /** The areas the group works, and the whole of what a run may change. */\n  areas: AreaName[];\n}\n\n/**\n * Parse one stored instruction.\n *\n * Strict JSON, an object at the top, then the fields checked: a `v` this build\n * does not know is refused rather than read as though it meant the same, an\n * instruction that is not text or says nothing is refused rather than carried\n * into a call as a heading over nothing, and an area nobody has is refused with\n * the names there are. A key this build does not know is ignored, so a field a\n * later build added decides nothing here.\n */\nexport function parseInstructionDocumentDetailed(\n  raw: string,\n): { instruction: InstructionDoc } | { problem: string } {\n  let whole: unknown;\n  try {\n    whole = JSON.parse(raw);\n  } catch (err) {\n    return { problem: `Not valid JSON${errorDetail(err)}.` };\n  }\n  if (!isRecord(whole)) return { problem: \"The document must be a JSON object.\" };\n  /* A document written before the areas existed says the prose alone: it is the\n     instruction it was, with no area declared, and nothing is invented for it. */\n  if (whole.v === 1) {\n    if (typeof whole.instruction !== \"string\" || !whole.instruction.trim())\n      return { problem: '\"instruction\" must say how the group wants its agent to work.' };\n    return {\n      instruction: { v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: whole.instruction, areas: [] },\n    };\n  }\n  if (whole.v !== INSTRUCTION_VERSION)\n    return {\n      problem: `\"v\" is ${JSON.stringify(whole.v)}; this build reads version ${INSTRUCTION_VERSION}.`,\n    };\n  if (typeof whole.instruction !== \"string\" || !whole.instruction.trim())\n    return { problem: '\"instruction\" must say how the group wants its agent to work.' };\n  if (!Array.isArray(whole.areas) || whole.areas.some((one) => typeof one !== \"string\"))\n    return { problem: '\"areas\" must be a list of area names.' };\n  const areas = declaredAreas(whole.areas as string[]);\n  if (areas.problem) return { problem: areas.problem };\n  return {\n    instruction: {\n      v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION,\n      instruction: whole.instruction,\n      areas: [...areas.areas],\n    },\n  };\n}\n","path":"/home/remote/git/gilbert/server/src/shared/instruction.ts"}

/**
 * A group's standing instruction, against the mock Stalwart (ADR 0031).
 *
 * What is pinned here is the one mechanism the design rests on: the document a
 * group wrote is read from its own account and carried as the middle of the
 * three levels, and a document this build cannot read is refused with its path
 * rather than read as an instruction that says nothing.
 */

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { after, before, test } from "node:test";
import {
  type Ctx,
  destroyAppNode,
  filesAccountId,
  readAppFileAt,
  writeAppBytesAt,
  writeAppFileAt,
} from "../appFolder.js";
import { freePort, waitForPort } from "../testkit.js";

const PORT = await freePort();
process.env.MOCK_PORT = String(PORT);
process.env.MOCK_USER = "demo@example.com";
process.env.MOCK_PASS = "demo-password";
process.env.STALWART_URL = `http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}`;
process.env.APP_SECRET = "test-secret-for-instruction";

const mock = await import("../mock/index.js");
const { fetchUpstreamSession } = await import("../upstream.js");
const {
  INSTRUCTION_FILE,
  INSTRUCTION_VERSION,
  InstructionError,
  parseInstructionDocumentDetailed,
  readInstruction,
} = await import("./instruction.js");

const BASE = `http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}`;
const AUTH = `Basic ${Buffer.from("demo@example.com:demo-password").toString("base64")}`;

let ctx: Ctx;
let accountId: string;

before(async () => {
  await waitForPort(BASE, AUTH);
  const session = await fetchUpstreamSession(AUTH, BASE);
  ctx = { authorization: AUTH, session, username: "demo@example.com" };
  accountId = filesAccountId(ctx);
  assert.ok(accountId, "the demo account owns Files");
});

after(() => {
  (mock as { server?: { close(): void } }).server?.close();
});

/** The stored document taken out again, so a test leaves the account as it found it. */
async function removeStored(): Promise<void> {
  const found = await readAppFileAt(ctx, accountId, INSTRUCTION_FILE);
  const id = found?.file.id;
  if (typeof id === "string") await destroyAppNode(ctx, accountId, id, {});
}

test("a group's instruction is read from its own account, and no document is no level", async () => {
  await removeStored();
  assert.equal(
    await readInstruction(ctx, accountId),
    null,
    "a group that has written no instruction carries no middle level",
  );

  await writeAppFileAt(ctx, accountId, INSTRUCTION_FILE, {
    v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION,
    instruction: "Answer the shipper in the group's own words.",
  });
  assert.equal(
    await readInstruction(ctx, accountId),
    "Answer the shipper in the group's own words.",
    "and one it wrote is read whole",
  );
  await removeStored();
});

test("an instruction this build cannot read is refused with its path, never carried as silence", async () => {
  for (const unreadable of [
    "{ not json",
    JSON.stringify({ v: 99, instruction: "anything" }),
    JSON.stringify({ v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: "   " }),
  ]) {
    await writeAppBytesAt(
      ctx,
      accountId,
      INSTRUCTION_FILE,
      new TextEncoder().encode(unreadable),
      "application/json",
    );
    await assert.rejects(
      () => readInstruction(ctx, accountId),
      (err: unknown) =>
        err instanceof InstructionError &&
        err.code === "instruction_unreadable" &&
        err.message.includes(INSTRUCTION_FILE),
      `a document that is ${unreadable} is refused as unreadable`,
    );
  }
  await removeStored();
});

test("the parser takes the version this build writes and refuses every other shape", () => {
  assert.deepEqual(
    parseInstructionDocumentDetailed(
      JSON.stringify({ v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: "Work by these words." }),
    ),
    { instruction: { v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: "Work by these words." } },
    "the shape this build writes parses whole",
  );
  assert.deepEqual(
    parseInstructionDocumentDetailed(
      JSON.stringify({
        v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION,
        instruction: "Work by these words.",
        retired: true,
      }),
    ),
    { instruction: { v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: "Work by these words." } },
    "a key this build does not know decides nothing and is dropped",
  );
  for (const raw of [
    "[]",
    JSON.stringify({ v: 2, instruction: "x" }),
    JSON.stringify({ v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION }),
    JSON.stringify({ v: INSTRUCTION_VERSION, instruction: 7 }),
  ]) {
    const parsed = parseInstructionDocumentDetailed(raw);
    assert.ok("problem" in parsed, `${raw} is refused`);
  }
});

function noRuleNotice(
  surface: "chat" | "mail",
  about: { from?: string | null; subject?: string | null } = {},
): string {

}

function noRuleNotice(
  surface: "chat" | "mail",
  about: { from?: string | null; subject?: string | null } = {},
): string {
  const where = surface === "mail" ? "mail" : "the conversation";
  const from = about.from ? ` from ${about.from}` : "";
  const subject = about.subject ? ` (“${about.subject}”)` : "";
  return `This group has no instruction naming ${where}, so the message${from}${subject} has woken nothing. An administrator can write one in Administration → Agent → Instruction.`;
}

/**
 * Whether the group's instruction names this change: its area is one the
 * instruction declares, or the surface is one its matrix does not turn off.
 *
 * The instruction is the whole of the routing (ADR 0038): a group that wrote no
 * area for mail is not woken by mail, and the notice above says so rather than
 * leaving the change unanswered in silence.
 */
function coversChange(instruction: InstructionDoc, event: AccountEvent): boolean {
  const area = areaOfSource(event.source);
  if (area === null) return false;
  if (instruction.areas.includes(area)) return true;
  const surface = event.source === "workorder" ? "workorder" : event.source;
  const mode = (instruction.surfaces as Record<string, string | undefined>)[surface];
  return mode !== undefined && mode !== "off";
}

    },

test("an answer that is not the demanded shape is refused, never guessed at", async () => {
  const cases: Array<[unknown, string]> = [
    ["not an object", "must be a JSON object"],
    [{ summary: "I decided something" }, 'exactly one of "rules" and "facts"'],
    [{ rules: ["shipper-answer"] }, '"facts" must be an object'],
    [{ rules: "shipper-answer", facts: {} }, '"rules" must be a list of rule names'],
    [
      { rules: ["shipper-answer", ""], facts: {} },
      '"rules" must be a list of rule names',
    ],
    [{ rules: [42], facts: {} }, '"rules" must be a list of rule names'],
    [{ rules: [], facts: { shipper: 42 } }, "values are text"],
    [
      { rules: ["shipper-answer", "shipper-answer"], facts: {} },
      '"rules" must name each rule at most once',
    ],
    // A rule named is not a rule run twice: the answer is refused rather than
    // read as a second run over the same change.
    [
      { rules: ["shipper-answer"], facts: {}, authority: "outward" },
      "what may be done is never the model's to say",

    // or a capability, is refused as the shape it is not.
    [
      { rules: ["shipper-answer"], facts: {}, actions: [{ do: "mail.send" }] },
      "never the model's to say",

      { read: { tool: "files.list" }, capability: "mail.send" },
      "An answer that reads carries nothing beside",

/** A rule whose matrix watches `watch` and leaves the other surfaces on demand. */
function ruleOf(
  id: string,
  watch: Array<keyof RuleDoc["surfaces"]> = ["mail"],
  instruction = "A shipper's message is answered within the day.",
): RuleDoc {
  const surfaces: RuleDoc["surfaces"] = {
    chat: "watch",
    mail: "ondemand",
    files: "ondemand",
    knowledge: "ondemand",
    workorder: "ondemand",
    calendar: "ondemand",
  };
  for (const surface of watch) surfaces[surface] = "watch";
  surfaces.chat = "watch";
  return { v: RULE_VERSION, id, surfaces, instruction, sends: false };
}

/** The group's rule, and the change in its account that wakes it. */

/** The holder every test but the claim's uses. */
const HOLDER = "process-a";
/** Every holder a test takes the claim for, so each one starts free. */
const HOLDERS = [HOLDER, "process-peer"];
/** The rules this test wrote, taken back out when it is over. */
const written: string[] = [];
/** The facts this test's runs wrote into the installation's memory. */
const remembered: string[] = [];

/**
 * Each test starts with no call seen, no answer queued, and the installation's
 * claim free — the claim is one document for the whole account, so a test that
 * left it held would stop the next one working.
 */
beforeEach(async () => {
  freshCalls();
  for (const holder of HOLDERS) await releaseClaim(ctx, holder);
  /*
   * Each test is a process meeting an account it has not read: the cursor is a
   * document now (ADR 0037), so the one a previous test wrote is taken out
   * before this one's first pass — otherwise this test reads the last test's
   * changes instead of its own.
   */
  const cursor = await readAppFileAt(ctx, accountId, CURSOR_FILE);
  if (typeof cursor?.file.id === "string")
    await destroyAppNode(ctx, accountId, cursor.file.id, {});
});

/**
 * A rule lives in the account and outlives the test that wrote it, and every
 * rule watching a surface answers a later test's change: each one is removed
 * with the test that wrote it. The same goes for the facts a run remembered —
 * the memory is one store for the whole installation, so a fact left behind
 * would be recalled by every later test's calls.
 */
afterEach(async () => {
  for (const id of written.splice(0)) {
    const found = await readAppFileAt(ctx, accountId, rulePath(id));
    const nodeId = found?.file.id;
    if (typeof nodeId === "string") await destroyAppNode(ctx, accountId, nodeId, {});
  }
  for (const id of remembered.splice(0)) {
    const found = await readAppFileAt(ctx, memoryAccountId, factPath(id));
    const nodeId = found?.file.id;
    if (typeof nodeId === "string")
      await destroyAppNode(ctx, memoryAccountId, nodeId, {});
  }
  // A group's standing instruction outlives the test too, and every later call
  // of this account would carry it.
  const instruction = await readAppFileAt(ctx, accountId, INSTRUCTION_FILE);
  if (typeof instruction?.file.id === "string")
    await destroyAppNode(ctx, accountId, instruction.file.id, {});
});

/** Every test starts with no call seen and no answer queued. */
function freshCalls(): void {
  seen = [];
  answers = [];
  onCall = null;
}

/** A surface list a test asks a rule to watch. */

/** A rule this build writes, watching one surface, removed with its test. */
async function putRule(id: string, watches: WatchList = ["mail"]): Promise<void> {
  await createRule(ctx, accountId, rule(id, watches));
  written.push(id);
}

/** The run a rule started, or a failure naming what is missing. */
async function runOf(ruleId: string) {
  const records = await listRuns(ctx, accountId);
  const found = records.find((record) => record.run.startedBy.rule === ruleId);
  assert.ok(found, `a run started by "${ruleId}" should be in the account`);
  return found.run;
}

/** Whether the call is the decision turn rather than a choosing one. */
function isDecision(system: string): boolean {
  return system.includes("the rules the group wrote for it");
}

/** Whether the call is the one that reads a person's answer for what it authorises. */
function isAuthorisation(system: string): boolean {
  return system.includes("their own words authorise");
}

/**
 * Whether the group's instruction names this change: its area is one the
 * instruction declares, or the surface is one its matrix does not turn off.
 *
 * The instruction is the whole of the routing (ADR 0038): a group that wrote no
 * area for mail is not woken by mail, and the notice above says so rather than
 * leaving the change unanswered in silence.
 */
function coversChange(instruction: InstructionDoc, event: AccountEvent): boolean {
  const area = areaOfSource(event.source);
  if (area === null) return false;
  if (instruction.areas.includes(area)) return true;
  const surface = (
    event.source === "workorder" ? "workorder" : event.source
  ) as SurfaceName;
  return instruction.surfaces[surface] !== "off";
}

/** The three levels of prose, outermost first (ADR 0031). */
export const PROSE_LEVELS = ["installation", "group", "rule"] as const;

/** One level of prose, named by where it is written. */
export type ProseLevel = (typeof PROSE_LEVELS)[number];

/** What each level is, as the model is told it. */
const LEVEL_HEADINGS: Record<ProseLevel, string> = {
  installation: "The installation's own rules, from whoever runs it:",
  group: "The group's standing instruction, from its members:",
  rule: "The rule's own instruction:",
};

/** One level's block, or "" when that level says nothing. */
export function proseBlock(level: ProseLevel, text?: string): string {
  const body = (text ?? "").trim();
  if (!body) return "";
  return `${LEVEL_HEADINGS[level]}\n${body}`;
}

   * The first write of a new group is the case the route's token has to survive:
   * the folder is made by the write itself, and a token read before that is
   * stale by the time it is used. The panel sends the state it read, so this does
   * too — and the second write takes the state the first one left.
   */
  const base = `/api/admin/groups/${encodeURIComponent(TEAM)}/prose`;
  const opened = await call(base);
  assert.equal(opened.status, 200);
  const first = (opened.body as { state: string }).state;

  const rule = {
    v: 1,
    id: "shipper",
    watches: ["mail"],
    instruction: "Answer the shipper.",
    sends: false,
  };
  const wroteRule = await call(`${base}/rules/shipper`, {
    method: "PUT",
    body: JSON.stringify({ rule, ifInState: first }),
  });
  assert.equal(wroteRule.status, 200, JSON.stringify(wroteRule.body));

  const second = (await call(base)).body as { state: string };
  const wroteLine = await call(`${base}/instruction`, {
    method: "PUT",
    body: JSON.stringify({ instruction: "Be brief.", ifInState: second.state }),
  });
  assert.equal(wroteLine.status, 200, JSON.stringify(wroteLine.body));

  const prose = (await call(base)).body as {
    instruction: string;
    rules: Array<{ id: string; instruction: string }>;
  };
  assert.equal(prose.instruction, "Be brief.", "the line is read back as written");
  assert.equal(
    prose.rules.find((one) => one.id === "shipper")?.instruction,
    "Answer the shipper.",
    "and so is the rule",
  );
});

test("a rule name that is not a file name is refused as the caller's, not upstream's", async () => {
  /*
   * The id is the rule's file name; "All freight" has a space in it. That is a
   * 400 with the rule's own sentence — the caller typed it and can fix it — not
   * the 502 an unmatched error becomes.
   */
  const base = `/api/admin/groups/${encodeURIComponent(TEAM)}/prose`;
  const state = ((await call(base)).body as { state: string }).state;
  const res = await call(`${base}/rules/${encodeURIComponent("All freight")}`, {
    method: "PUT",
    body: JSON.stringify({
      rule: {
        v: 1,
        id: "All freight",
        watches: ["mail"],
        instruction: "Answer the shipper.",
        sends: false,
      },
      ifInState: state,
    }),
  });
  assert.equal(res.status, 400);
  assert.equal((res.body as { error: string }).error, "rule_id_invalid");
});

/**
 * The prose that reaches the model, and the order it reaches it in (ADR 0031).
 *
 * The three levels are the installation's own line, the group's standing
 * instruction and the rule's own instruction, and the record names them
 * outermost first. This test is the whole of that order: it fixes the levels
 * and their sequence, so the builder's order cannot move without it. It is the
 * one pin on that order, and the reason it is a test rather than a comment:
 * swapping two levels produces a prompt that reads as though the rule
 * outranked the installation, and nothing else in the tree would notice.
 */

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { test } from "node:test";
import { PROSE_LEVELS, proseBlock, proseForModel } from "./prose.js";

test("the model is told the three levels outermost first", () => {
  const blocks = proseForModel({
    installation: "Never write as a person.",
    group: "Answer in the group's own language.",
    rule: "A shipper's message is answered within the day.",
  });

    blocks,

      "The group's standing instruction, from its members:\nAnswer in the group's own language.",
      "The rule's own instruction:\nA shipper's message is answered within the day.",
    ],
    "the order is the record's: the installation, the group, the rule",
  );
  assert.deepEqual(
    [...PROSE_LEVELS],
    ["installation", "group", "rule"],
    "and the order is stated once, outermost first",
  );
});

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { test } from "node:test";
import type { RunStep } from "../shared/run.js";
import type { DecisionQuestion, StepQuestion } from "./model.js";
import {
  READ_IN_PROMPT_MAX,
  STEP_OUTCOME_FULL_MAX,
  STEP_OUTCOME_OLD_MAX,
  stepData,
  turnData,
} from "./prompt.js";

/**
 * The prompt is paid for by the token and bounded by the provider's context: a
 * lookup that answered a large document is clipped, and the cut is visible in
 * the text rather than a call that fails at the provider.
 */
test("a lookup larger than the prompt's bound is clipped, and says so", () => {
  const question = {
    event: { source: "mail", change: "created", where: "m-1" },
  } as DecisionQuestion;
  const huge = "a".repeat(READ_IN_PROMPT_MAX + 500);
  const prompt = turnData(question, [], [{ name: "files.read", result: { text: huge } }]);

  assert.ok(prompt.length < huge.length, "the whole document is not in the prompt");
  assert.ok(prompt.includes("…"), "and the reader can see it was cut");
  assert.ok(
    prompt.includes("a".repeat(1_000)),
    "what is carried is the answer's own beginning",
  );
});

/** One ended step whose outcome is longer than the prompt carries of an old one. */
function ended(at: number, state: RunStep["state"] = "done"): RunStep {
  return {
    what: `step-${at} action`,
    state,
    outcome: `${at}:${"x".repeat(STEP_OUTCOME_OLD_MAX * 4)}`,
    needs: null,
  };

});

/**
 * One decision turn: given a change and the group's rules, which rules apply
 * and what are the facts.
 *
 * The candidates are the rules whose watch covers the change (`ruleApplies`) and
 * nothing else, so the watch a rule declares is enforced here rather than
 * trusted to the model. A change no rule watches is decided without a call at
 * all — and without a bill. Every candidate that fits the change is named and
 * runs: a change two rules cover is the group's own decision, so the model
 * chooses between no two of them (ADR 0031).
 *
 * The model may look the group's own state up with the **reading tools** before
 * it answers, up to `DECISION_READS_MAX` times; each read is run through
 * `runTool` over `READING_TOOLS`, so a tool that changes the account is not in
 * the catalogue to be named and the authority guard (`mayRun`) is the one that
 * answers every call. The answer is validated before it is returned: a malformed
 * answer, or one naming a rule the group did not write, is refused rather than
 * guessed at.

/**
 * The agent's areas — ADR 0038.
 *
 * Each area is a module of tools with one concern: posta, files, calendario,
 * contatti, conoscenza, workorder, chat, memoria. A run is handed **the areas its
 * change and its instruction declare**, plus the three that every run needs —
 * chat (the interface), conoscenza (the shared library) and memoria (what the
 * installation knows).
 *
 * This file is the one place that says which area a tool belongs to: a new tool
 * names its area here, and nothing else in the tree repeats the mapping. The
 * catalogue a turn sees is computed from it, so the model never again reads
 * forty-five names to use four.
 */

import { AREA_NAMES, type AreaName, TRANSVERSAL_AREAS } from "../shared/areas.js";
import type { SurfaceMatrix } from "../shared/surfaces.js";

export {
  AREA_NAMES,
  type AreaName,
  declaredAreas,
  isAreaName,
  MAX_DECLARED_AREAS,
  TRANSVERSAL_AREAS,
} from "../shared/areas.js";

/** A tool's prefix where the area's own name differs from it. */
const AREA_ALIASES: Readonly<Record<string, AreaName>> = { workorder: "workorders" };

/**
 * Prefixes that name no area: the agent's own record (`run.read`), which every
 * run may consult, is a tool of the harness rather than of a product surface.
 */
export const CONTEXT_TOOL_PREFIXES: readonly string[] = ["run"];

function prefixOf(toolName: string): string | null {
  const dot = toolName.indexOf(".");
  return dot > 0 ? toolName.slice(0, dot) : null;
}

/** Whether a tool belongs to an area rather than to the harness. */
export function isAreaTool(toolName: string): boolean {
  const prefix = prefixOf(toolName);
  if (prefix === null) return false;
  return (
    AREA_ALIASES[prefix] !== undefined ||
    (AREA_NAMES as readonly string[]).includes(prefix)
  );
}

/**
 * The area a tool belongs to, from its name's own prefix.
 *
 * A tool's name is `area.action` by construction (the catalogue's naming rule),
 * so the mapping is read and not maintained twice. A name that matches no area is
 * a defect in the tool, and it is refused here rather than silently handed to
 * every run.
 */
export function areaOf(toolName: string): AreaName {
  const prefix = prefixOf(toolName);
  if (prefix === null)
    throw new Error(
      `The tool "${toolName}" names no area: its name must be area.action, with area one of ${AREA_NAMES.join(", ")}.`,
    );
  const alias = AREA_ALIASES[prefix];
  if (alias !== undefined) return alias;
  const found = AREA_NAMES.find((area) => area === prefix);
  if (!found)
    throw new Error(
      `The tool "${toolName}" names no area: its name must start with one of ${AREA_NAMES.join(", ")}.`,
    );
  return found;
}

/** One group's standing instruction, as it is stored. */
export interface InstructionDoc {
  /** The schema version; `INSTRUCTION_VERSION` today. */
  v: 2;
  /** In prose, how the group wants its agent to work. */
  instruction: string;

  /** Where a run may act, one mode per surface of the group's own account. */

export async function findFolderPath(
  ctx: Ctx,
  accountId: string,
  path: string,
): Promise<string | null> {
  let current = await findAppFolder(ctx, accountId);
  if (!current) return null;
  for (const segment of pathSegments(path)) {
    const children = await fileChildren(ctx, accountId, current, FOLDER_PROPS);
    const found = children.find((n) => n.nodeType === "directory" && n.name === segment);
    if (!found?.id) return null;
    current = String(found.id);
  }
  return current;
}

 * and the server writes as the Master, behind the same door as the rest of the
 * administration. That is what makes the decision a boundary rather than a
 * hidden button.
 *
 * The shapes are the server's own (`@gilbert/agent/rule`,
 * `@gilbert/shared/instruction`), the documents are validated by the server's
 * parser, and the write is a compare-and-set: the state a read answered is sent
 * back, and a write whose account moved under it is refused with 409.
 */

import type { RuleDoc } from "@gilbert/agent/rule";
import { apiFetch } from "@/jmap/client";

/** One group's prose, as the route answers it. */
export interface GroupProse {
  instruction: string;
  rules: RuleDoc[];
  /** The account's FileNode state the read saw: what a write is conditioned on. */
  state: string;
}

function prosePath(group: string, rest = ""): string {
  return `/api/admin/groups/${encodeURIComponent(group)}/prose${rest}`;
}

/** Read a group's standing instruction and its rules. */
export async function readGroupProse(group: string): Promise<GroupProse> {
  return await apiFetch<GroupProse>(prosePath(group));
}

/** Save the standing instruction; an emptied field leaves no document behind. */
export async function saveInstruction(
  group: string,
  text: string,
  state?: string,
): Promise<void> {
  await apiFetch(prosePath(group, "/instruction"), {
    method: "PUT",
    body: JSON.stringify({ instruction: text, ...(state ? { ifInState: state } : {}) }),
  });
}

That is\n * what makes the decision a boundary rather than a hidden button.\n *\n * The shapes are the server's own (`@gilbert/shared/instruction` and\n * `@gilbert/shared/areas`), the document is validated by the server's parser,\n * and the write is a compare-and-set: the state a read answered is sent back,\n * and a write whose account moved under it is refused with 409.\n */\n\nimport type { AreaName } from \"@gilbert/shared/areas\";\nimport { apiFetch } from \"@/jmap/client\";\n\n/** One group's instruction, as the route answers it. */\nexport interface GroupInstruction {\n  instruction: string;\n  /** The areas the group works: the whole of what a run may change. */\n  areas: AreaName[];\n  /** The account's FileNode state the read saw: what a write is conditioned on. */\n  state: string;\n}\n\nfunction prosePath(group: string, rest = \"\"): string {\n  return `/api/admin/groups/${encodeURIComponent(group)}/prose${rest}`;\n}\n\n/** Read a group's instruction and the areas it works. */\nexport async function readGroupInstruction(group: string): Promise<GroupInstruction> {\n  return await apiFetch<GroupInstruction>(prosePath(group));\n}\n\n/** Save the instruction and its areas; an emptied field leaves no document behind. */\nexport async function saveInstruction(\n  group: string,\n  text: string,\n  areas: readonly AreaName[],\n  state?: string,\n): Promise<void> {\n  await apiFetch(prosePath(group, \"/instruction\"), {\n    method: \"PUT\",\n    body: JSON.stringify({\n      instruction: text,\n      areas,\n      ...(state ? { ifInState: state } : {}),\n    }),\n  });\n}\n","path":"/home/remote/git/gilbert/web/src/lib/agentProse.ts"}

/** The document's name for a rule, from the name a person typed. */
function ruleIdFrom(name: string): string {
  return name
    .normalize("NFKD")
    .replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, "")
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9._-]+/g, "-")
    .replace(/^[-.]+|[-.]+$/g, "")
    .replace(/-{2,}/g, "-");
}

/**
 * One rule's editor: the name (only while it is new), the surfaces it watches,
 * what should happen, and whether it declares that it sends.
 */
function RuleEditor({
  initial,
  onSave,
  onDelete,
  onCancel,
}: {
  initial: RuleDoc;
  onSave(rule: RuleDoc, create: boolean): Promise<void>;
  onDelete?(): Promise<void>;
  onCancel?(): void;
}) {
  const existing = Boolean(onDelete);
  const [id, setId] = useState(initial.id);
  const [surfaces, setSurfaces] = useState<RuleSurfaces>(initial.surfaces);
  const [instruction, setInstruction] = useState(initial.instruction);
  const [sends, setSends] = useState(initial.sends);
  /*
   * The name is a person's; the id is the document's file name, derived from it
   * so a space or an accent is never something the reader has to work around.
   */
  const ruleId = existing ? id : ruleIdFrom(id);
  /** A name with a letter or a digit in it can become a rule. */
  const validId = ruleId.length > 0;
  const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const setMode = (
    surface: Exclude<(typeof RULE_SURFACES)[number], "chat">,
    mode: SurfaceMode,
  ) => {
    setSurfaces((held) => ({ ...held, [surface]: mode }));
  };

  const act = async (work: () => Promise<void>) => {
    setBusy(true);
    setError(null);
    try {
      await work();
    } catch (err) {
      setError(errorMessage(err));
    } finally {
      setBusy(false);
    }
  };

  return (
    <div className="field" style={{ border: "1px solid var(--border)", padding: 12 }}>
      {existing ? (
        <strong>{id}</strong>
      ) : (
        <div className="field">
          <label htmlFor="new-rule-id">{t("Rule name")}</label>
          <input
            id="new-rule-id"
            value={id}
            placeholder={t("All freight")}

import { RULE_SURFACES, RULE_VERSION } from "@gilbert/agent/rule";
import { INSTRUCTION_VERSION } from "@gilbert/shared/instruction";
import { expect, it } from "vitest";

/**
 * The agent's document shapes, as a surface writes them (ADR 0031).
 *
 * A group's rules and its standing instruction are the group's own documents, so
 * the client writes them with the group's session — and it writes them in the
 * shape the server reads. That shape is one definition, in the agent's tree, and
 * the alias `@gilbert/agent/*` is what lets this tier read it instead of
 * spelling a second one. The import above is the assertion: a second definition
 * would not resolve here at all.
 *
 * The version a document carries is the agent's to move, and a test that pinned
 * it would break on the day a rule gains a field rather than on the day the two
 * tiers disagreed; what is pinned is the surfaces the editor draws, which is the
 * client's own contract with the shape.
 */
it("a surface reads the agent's shapes from the one definition", () => {
  expect(Number.isInteger(RULE_VERSION)).toBe(true);
  expect(RULE_VERSION).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
  expect(Number.isInteger(INSTRUCTION_VERSION)).toBe(true);
  expect(RULE_SURFACES).toEqual([
    "chat",
    "mail",
    "files",
    "knowledge",
    "workorder",
    "calendar",
  ]);
});

import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from "vitest";

/**
 * A group's prose is written through the administration's route, not the group's
 * account (owner decision 2026-10-18). What this tier owns is the call: the
 * group's name in the path, and the state the read answered carried back on every
 * write so the server can refuse one that lost a race.
 */
const { apiFetch } = vi.hoisted(() => ({ apiFetch: vi.fn() }));
vi.mock("@/jmap/client", () => ({ apiFetch }));

import { deleteRule, readGroupProse, saveInstruction, saveRule } from "../agentProse";

const GROUP = "team@example.org";
const PATH = "/api/admin/groups/team%40example.org/prose";

beforeEach(() => {
  apiFetch.mockReset();
});

describe("the prose route", () => {
  it("reads the instruction, the rules and the state", async () => {
    apiFetch.mockResolvedValue({
      instruction: "Answer in the group's voice.",
      rules: [{ id: "invoices" }],
      state: "s7",
    });
    const prose = await readGroupProse(GROUP);
    expect(apiFetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith(PATH);
    expect(prose.state).toBe("s7");
    expect(prose.rules).toHaveLength(1);
  });

  it("carries the state the read answered back on a write", async () => {
    apiFetch.mockResolvedValue({ ok: true });
    await saveInstruction(GROUP, "Answer in the group's voice.", "s7");
    expect(apiFetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith(`${PATH}/instruction`, {
      method: "PUT",
      body: JSON.stringify({
        instruction: "Answer in the group's voice.",
        ifInState: "s7",
      }),
    });

    apiFetch.mockResolvedValue({ rule: { id: "invoices" } });
    await saveRule(GROUP, { id: "invoices" } as never, "s7");
    expect(apiFetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith(`${PATH}/rules/invoices`, {
      method: "PUT",
      body: JSON.stringify({ rule: { id: "invoices" }, ifInState: "s7" }),
    });

    apiFetch.mockResolvedValue({ ok: true });
    await deleteRule(GROUP, "invoices", "s7");
    expect(apiFetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith(`${PATH}/rules/invoices`, {
      method: "DELETE",
      body: JSON.stringify({ ifInState: "s7" }),
    });
  });
});

## A group's engagement is a rule in prose

**A group's engagement is a rule in prose** (ADR 0031): one document in the
group's own account, under `rules/`, that gives each of the account's surfaces a
**mode** — **off**, **watch** or **on demand** — and says in prose what should
happen when the rule is woken. The surfaces are its **chat**, its **mail**, its
**KB**, its **workorders**, its **Files** and its **calendar**; chat is always
**watch**, because the conversation is where the group calls the agent and where
its report is written. **watch** wakes the rule and lets the run it opens write
that surface; on **mail** that means a message that **arrived in the Inbox** —
reading, marking, filing or removing a message wakes nothing, and neither does a
draft the group saved or a message it sent; **on demand** never wakes it but lets
a run already open — from chat, from mail, from another watched surface — write
it; **off** neither wakes nor writes (reading stays free). The matrix says
*where* a run may act, never *what*: the authority classes (ADR 0028) still bound
every act, and a write on a surface the rule keeps off is refused
(`surface_off`). The run carries the matrix its rule had when it opened, so an
edit does not move a run in flight; a v1 rule is read as the matrix it means
(watched surfaces `watch`, the rest `ondemand`)
and is written as v2 on the next save. The shape, its parser and the matrix's
matcher are `server/src/agent/rule.ts`, the modes are
`server/src/shared/surfaces.ts`, and where a rule lives is
`server/src/agent/rules.ts`. A rule may **declare that it sends**, which is the
one power it carries of its own. The agent's prose has three
levels, outermost first: the **installation's own line**, the **group's standing
instruction** and the **rule's own instruction**, and one builder,
`server/src/agent/prose.ts`, produces that order for every caller. The first is
`agent.instruction` in the installation's own document, carried into every call
from the boot; the second is `instruction.json` in the group's own account
(`server/src/agent/instruction.ts`), read once per pass so an edit is in force at
the next one; the third is re-read for each turn of the run it started. A level
that says nothing contributes nothing. **An installation administrator decides**
the group's two documents, from **Administration → AI Agents → Prose**: the group
is chosen, the standing instruction is one field, and a rule is its name, its
matrix, its prose and whether it may send. The launcher is offered
only to an administrator, and the write goes through the administration's own
route (`/api/admin/groups/<name>/prose`), which writes as the Master behind
`requireAdmin` — the decision is a boundary and not a hidden button (owner
decision 2026-10-18). Each document is validated by the server's parser before it
is filed, and every write carries the account state the read answered, so a write
that lost a race is refused rather than overwriting another administrator's edit.
The installation's own line is a field beside its model in Administration →
Installation, and it is read at every pass.

## One model, two turns

**One model serves the installation** (ADR 0027), chosen in Administration and
stored in the installation's own document with a **write-only** key: a read of a
document this build can parse takes the key out of it, while a document that is
not JSON is handed back byte for byte so a person can repair it by hand; a save
that states no key keeps the stored one, and the switch for a provider that
needs none clears it. `server/src/agent/model.ts` posts one OpenAI-compatible chat
completion with the zero-retention opt-out on every request, refuses a provider
whose address is not public unless the **operator** has said the installation's
model may sit inside the deployment's own network
(`GILBERT_AGENT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_PROVIDER`), and carries both turns: the **decision
turn** — given one change in a group's own account and the rules that watch it,
which rules apply and what the facts are, looking the group's own state up first
with the **reading tools** when it needs to — and the **choosing turn**, which is
handed the catalogue as the catalogue describes itself — the provider's own
`tools`, each rendered from the tool's own argument specs, once per call and never
repeated as prose — and
the run so far, and
answers with a **plan**: one or more steps, each a tool, its arguments and what it

and what follows from each outcome, is one turn. A provider that takes the tools
